utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't mean to slow things down at all, but a brief issue. At the end of the day yesterday, you ordered us by noon to do the annex to our request for assistance -- excuse me, for our Rule 54 petition, and we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And per the order of the Court, we could not discuss -- or we did not contact Mr. Jenkins, but he actually made the request to (redacted) on our behalf, and so we would need that annex from him, and we need it to do that, so what we hope to do is if you'd just give us leave to -- at the first break to make arrangements, I think, by accessing e-mails and whatnot we can make that happen. But that was the one thing we want to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll give you that leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. O'Leary, I was once a young Prosecutor, and nothing annoyed me more than to come to court with my own strategy for leading the evidence worked out and to be told by the judge to adopt another approach. What I would suggest is that we stop hearing from Mr. Jenkins about the general principles of investigation and take him straight directly to the areas that he identifies as weaknesses in the Prosecution's investigation, and in particular, if he's able to, to say why that particular method would tend to make the evidence gathered unreliable because ultimately that is what we will be interested in. So let him go immediately to the house and say, I saw this, or I didn't see this, and this is not in accordance with general accepted practice; but more important than that for us, whether it is in accordance with his own practice, is why it is unreliable, why the evidence gathered is unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would it be acceptable if we go site by site?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll proceed that way. Oh, and I believe we need to go in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And I'm not certain if it is for other people, but the LiveNote is not working on our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jenkins.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Let's go back to where we ended your testimony yesterday, then. If we go site by site, I believe we were at Pionirska yesterday.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: So let's just start back with what were you looking for at Pionirska that you thought should be included in an investigative report?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence we were looking for would be -- would be anything that would either prove or disprove that a fire or explosion was obvious to a trained eye once we had a chance to examine the scene and the evidence that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We had just discussed cross-contamination and a couple of things that could affect the reliability of evidence due to time. There were some other things you had mentioned in your report that could affect the evidence that could be collected at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could call up 1D22-0696. It's the photo index that was an addendum to your report. Page 3, please. That's actually the report. I'm looking for the addendum, which is 1D22-0696.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: While we look for the actual photograph, can you tell us other factors that you encountered at the site that would affect any evidence that would be collected to this stage?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I found the general condition of the crime scene had degraded to the point where any valuable evidence that might be collected had probably reached the point where it was either totally destroyed or almost to that point. The crime scene was not in good shape at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What elemental factors did you take into consideration?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there appears to be -- of course, when we were there it was raining that weekend, and that room is obviously subjected to a large amount of water. The floors are muddy. The walls have almost deteriorated to the point where I would not want to go back in there for an extended period of time and conduct a search for fear that the building is about to collapse. I would want -- before we went in and did an extensive examination of the floor area of Pionirska, I would want an engineer to go in and ensure me that that building was safe enough that we could conduct that search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does that affect any item of evidence that you know the Prosecution would have relied on to prove its case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the problem with that, Your Honour, is that that moisture has a tendency, for example, to wash the walls. It caused the concrete along the side of the walls to degenerate, and I think when we get the photo array or the photos up, you'll see that it's to the point where if you were to take your index finger and brush along the wall, the concrete disintegrates against your finger. That's how degraded that concrete is, and it's due to the water washing away the minerals in the concrete. How it affects the evidence is, say for example there is a fire, and there's going to be smoke residue along the walls, well, when the walls degenerate to that point, that evidence is lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Jenkins. Your Honours, the counsel has not laid a foundation for this witness to give any evidence as to fire and explosives and the residue of fire or anything of the kind. The question Your Honour has asked obviously about the site and the destruction of evidence perhaps falls in his purview, but I would object to any -- to -- without a foundation being laid, to this expert being asked questions as to relating to the cause of the fire, the origin of the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see why he shouldn't answer the question that I have asked. Please answer the question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And we found the document, and I'm sorry about that. It's 1D22-0705. It should be there at page 3, what we're discussing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue with the explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- in answer to counsellor's question, I'm really not interested in how the fire started. I'm merely speaking of the residue that would be left behind if such an event had taken place. And it could have been hypothetically, say there was someone building a pipe bomb, and the pipe bomb exploded, killing the individual that was building the bomb. There would be residue on the wall from that crime scene as well. And if it were in this situation and the wall degenerated, over a period of time that evidence would be lost on the floor. I hope that makes sense for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We have the pictures on the screen. We're referring to the top picture, which is listed as number 879. Can you tell us in that photograph what you're describing.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph of the south-east wall of the basement area of the alleged crime scene, and if the Tribunal will notice, in the upper right-hand corner there's a sort of green tint. That is mold that has attached itself to the wall, and the area that's to the centre and slightly down and to the right, you can see the white areas there in the centre. That is part of the wall that has fallen away, and I actually took my finger as I described before and brushed that wall below the area where that mold is, and the wall disintegrated against my finger, much like -- it's just degenerated to the point where it's very unstable.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And when was this photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The LiveNote, as you have indicated, is not working and I would like the technicians to attend to that as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Shall I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken on 29 January of '09.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And when would this start to affect the scene? How long into after the actual events would it start to decompose in this manner that you've described?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say because it depends on how secure the roof was and for what period of time leading up to our visit at the scene, so without -- you know, there's really no way to answer that with any surety.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How much will it continue to deteriorate over time?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way it is right now, as I indicated earlier, if it continues deteriorating at this current rate, it won't take too much longer and these walls will give way, and the entire building will collapse.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I'm not sure how you want to deal with reports. My understanding was you wanted to have them taken at the end as far as admission, but perhaps we could mark for identification this photograph alone, since we've referred to it in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we could have 65 ter 18 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How much time did you spend at the Pionirska site on your site visit?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually visited the site on two consecutive days. On the morning of the 29th we were there, I would say, an hour and a half, maybe two hours; and on the second day, I asked if we could revisit the scene. I just wanted to revisit the site because I had a couple of questions in my own mind about things that I'd seen the day before, and I asked if we could revisit the site for a short period, and we were there maybe half an hour the second day.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Okay. And if you look at the screen now, you'll see an aerial shot. Do you know what this photograph is?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an aerial photograph of the area around the Pionirska scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And can you mark where you went for your Pionirska visit, with the court usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The scene, the Pionirska fire is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What other areas did you have -- actually, could you put a P by it for indicating that that is the Pionirska scene, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Could you tell us what other areas that you had opportunity to look at in this neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We also had -- from review of the documents, we had information about one of the witnesses that was located on a balcony approximately here. I'll mark that with a W, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question was presented whether or not the witness from this location could see the scene as reported in her statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And what else can you tell us generally about the neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there -- can I have a clear screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can I tender this marked exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And then if the court usher could bring up a blank screen, please. A blank screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the blank screen, perhaps I can explain what my intentions are --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: With the blank screen.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with the blank screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And by blank screen, I need to -- I need to be able to sketch, so I need to have this photograph removed and --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: They're saving it.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: While we're talking about that, or while we're waiting on that, can you tell us just a general indication of what type of a neighborhood is it, what is it --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the neighborhood of the Pionirska scene is located on the side of a hill. And the area to the north of the Pionirska scene, which is the area across the flood channel or the ditch, there are several houses that are located along that hill to the north that are approximately 3 to 5 metres higher than the Pionirska building, the home where the incident took place. That slope, actually at that point it sort of rises. There's a ridge or a saddle that runs right down next to the home, and then it continues to slope down towards the village of Visegrad. So it is -- if you were to look at it, if -- I'm going to do this backwards so it will give you some context to the Tribunal. But the homes above Pionirska would be here; there's a flood channel that runs immediately adjacent to the home on Pionirska, the Pionirska scene; then we have the home. Then there's the other bank of the flood control channel, and then there's a slight saddle or a hump that runs right along with those homes that we'll see here in a moment. Then it continues to fall off to the -- it would be to the south, the south-west.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure if we're -- okay, thank you. I believe you're free to mark on the screen now to indicate what you've just spoken about.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. And I beg your forgiveness, I'm not a very good artist, so -- if we're to look at the area, first of all, this is the flood control ditch, and for the sake of argument, let's put the scene here. This would be the Pionirska scene. So this is the ditch, water flowing in this direction. This bank is, say, 3 to 5 metres higher than this bank. There is a parking-lot or some sort of large driveway, patio area here, and the road that you've seen on the photographs runs like this. There is a road, a back road that runs here. There is a house here that is marked this way. That's supposed to be like a backwards 7. Then there is another home that extends almost all the way to the road, and then there's the balcony, and this is approximately the location where the witness was. Now, if we were to look at this in cross-section, what you would see is you would see the ditch coming down. Then there's the house with a slight hump, and then it falls back off to where these houses are located. So there's actually a small ridge that runs. So if you were to take your GPS unit, and most of the modern units will give you not only the latitude and longitude but also your altitude above sea level, if you were to shoot that, and I don't know exactly what the altitude is, but for the sake, again, of argument, let's just say that this is 1.000 feet, if you were to take the reading at the top of the parking area, it might say 1.003 feet. Back over here, it might say 1.000 feet again. So there's actually some obstruction because of the way the hill, that saddle comes through. If you're standing at ground level, you cannot see over that hump to what is happening in Pionirska at the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does that affect your take on this scene as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what it tells me is if -- even if there's a witness standing in close proximity, say to within even -- I would say within 15 metres of this ditch bank, you cannot see down into the entrance to that room. You have to physically get almost up to the edge of that bank to look down the hill to see what is in the -- what's going on at the scene. And again, I apologise for this chicken scratch. It's not very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move to admit this diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If we could call back up the addendum we just had, 1D22-0705, and go to page 7 this time, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, in relation to -- you did have access to where the witness had said she was on the evening of the Pionirska fire.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that location?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a two-storey building. It is, I would say, 250 to -- approximately 250 metres from the scene. But what is of note is that the house -- the neighbor's house totally obstructs the direct line of sight to the Pionirska scene, and in addition to that there's a 3-storey building on the other side of the main street that would also obstruct the view of the witness from her reported location.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the bottom photograph on that page, 894.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this picture is?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph of the balcony area that the witness was standing on.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And when was this taken?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken on 29 January of '09.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What can you see from this photograph in relation to the Pionirska incident?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Say again?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What can we see in this photograph in relation to the Pionirska incident?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The balcony that you see above the area that is coloured in kind of a yellow colour, that is the balcony area from which the witness is report to have been standing. If you look to the left, you can see the next-door residence and how that wall extends beyond parallel with the witness's back wall and thus obstructing any views back towards the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: May I ask a question? I'm sorry, but did the witness say she saw the fire or only the smoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe she said she saw the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: My recollection of what she said here in court was that she only saw the smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we'd get to what she was available to see from that location as we progress. It might help to go to page 9, the bottom picture there.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what are we seeing in this photograph here?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken from the balcony of the residence that was occupied by VG-115. This would be an accurate representation of what she was able to see from her balcony.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What views did she have from that point from that balcony?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What views did she have from that balcony?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: She has a view of the flood-control channel somewhere approximately 50 to 65 metres further to the west, so there is no direct line of sight with the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: On the evening of Pionirska, what could she see?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the weather conditions that were present at the time. If it were rainy or foggy, there could be some ambient light that would be reflected from a fire or, you know, similar incident that could be seen that far down the channel. But as far as any actual activity at the scene, you couldn't see from this location.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And to follow up with Your Honour's question, what about smoke? Could she have seen smoke from here?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's possible, depending on the wind. Certainly if smoke were to drift down the canyon that way, it could also reflect the light. Those are both possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'd like to mark for identification these two photos as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D211, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could call up 65 ter 178.59. And Your Honours, for transcript reference as far as VG-115's testimony, it does say -- it's in the question from the Prosecutor, actually, but it says: "Which house was torched where you saw the smoke coming from the fire and the flames which you saw?" And she says -- on the screen she marks the photograph so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel kindly speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this photograph is, Mr. Jenkins.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an aerial photograph of the scene at the Pionirska fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this photograph that's important to an investigation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. May I interrupt you. I seem to remember that this little confusion was caused by a question that was asked and not by what the witness said genuinely, because the question was which house was torched, and then she made a marking. It's not that she out of her own initiative said that she had seen the fire, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Right. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: And I think it may have been brought by that confusion and not the way you were saying it just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, and that's why I wanted to quote that directly. It was in the question, so I'm not exactly sure. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, in this house, what would be important to you to look at as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shrubberies, the surrounding out-buildings also play a role into the ability of the witness to see any of the activity at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what did you notice -- what did you notice of the shrubbery?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on our visit the shrubbery was no longer there. It's pretty much been cleaned out, as have those -- at least that one out-building that is directly next to the home. Those -- that building is no longer there, and the shrubs and trees are no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: So step by step, as an investigator, how would you process this scene?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this condition?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Today, as you saw it on the site visit.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The scene would be processed much in the same way -- the same way that we discussed yesterday. There would be a diagram of the scene drawn; evidence visually identified that we want to collect. There would be still photographs taken with a scale next to the items so we have an accurate measurement of the items that we're talking about or the items that we're going to take into evidence. And once everything is photographed and measured and the measurements of the room are memorialised on a sketch, then we would begin a systematic process of collecting that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My main interest is how does all of this, all of these shortcomings affect the Prosecution case, because we're not conducting an investigation into the Prosecution's investigative techniques.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a university seminar, you know. I want to know how it affects the case that the Prosecution has presented. That's how Mr. Lukic will benefit from this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you can show me that the failure on the part of the Prosecution in collecting particular items of evidence renders the case less credible, less reliable. It's not a -- I don't want to hear a general theory about how the investigation should be conducted, although of course the Chamber might have something to say about that in its judgement ultimately, but that's not really the main purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: My next question, then, and I hope this answers your question, but why does it matter in this incident that these steps had been taken?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply because as soon as practical, the investigator should have taken this evidence to prevent it from being further destroyed, and we have no idea what evidence was there, whether it would benefit either the Prosecution or the Defence. We have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What evidence in this case could still be collected today?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a possibility that there are bone fragments in the dirt. There's a possibility that there are bullets or bullet fragments in the dirt. Potentially, there could be -- there could be documents. There could be clothing. There could be some things in the soil that would help identify any of the victims if there were any. It would help establish that in fact there was a fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why don't we have these materials right now?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, why don't we have?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why don't we have these materials?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What effect does it have on an overall investigation to not have these materials?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it speaks directly to whether or not the crime even occurred. If there's no evidence, no bodies, it's difficult to make that assertion and carry it forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And I think we can move on then to Bikavac, which if we call up 1D00-0021.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What can you tell -- how much time did you spend at the Bikavac scene?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent, I would say, 45 minutes to an hour there. That particular crime scene is open, and it has degenerated to the point where there really wasn't much for us to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the scene as you saw it in January, I believe?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The scene at this point is really nothing more than a neighborhood garbage dump.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does that affect an investigation?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any evidence that may be left behind is buried beneath several inches of trash. It would take a considerable effort to unearth.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Before we get into that, can you quickly mark on the map here where you were looking as the Bikavac incident scene.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's approximately where this X is, as near as I can tell. I believe it's right in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us about this terrain?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this photograph is somewhat deceiving. From this aerial photograph, it looks like it's a nice meadow, but in fact it's located on the side of a hill that I would estimate it probably a 6- to 7-degree incline.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does that affect an investigation?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the forensic side of it, it wouldn't affect it at all. From the prospect of the witnesses, it may or may not be relevant depending -- you know, the witness was severely burned and was running around, you know, that area, and that's -- I won't say it's impossible to run up and down those hills, but it would -- it's pretty steep.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about these roads?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're very narrow. The road -- you really can't even see a road. There's actually a road that leads back into this scene, that cuts back in here, and then there's another road -- at least the way the scene is now, there's another road like this, and two cars on this road could not pass each other, and this road also dead-ends here. There's a T-intersection here, and up in this area, it seems like the road services these house, but I could not observe the road going any further up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And by the way, this road is hardly categorised as a road, this particular road right here. It is really more of a trail. It is a -- it almost looks like a rutted access road. It's very -- very narrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Can you give any indication of what is the distance between the house you've indicated as the main road that's moving sort of diagonally?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the scene back -- from the scene here back to this road is probably 10 metres, 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And how much is the distance from the scene to the main road that's running diagonally?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: From the juncture at that main road there?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From here --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If you could indicate --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From here to here, I would estimate just an estimation of about 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. I could be in error. That could actually be a little bit further. If I were to convert the -- and I'm sorry, but I'm not used to working in metres, but I would estimate, if the Tribunal will indulge me, in feet, I would say that would be somewhere in the area of 350 to 400 feet back to the main road, and I'm sorry I'm not quick enough to do the conversion.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jenkins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have the same deficiency.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could tender that map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could call up 65 ter 178.67.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Would it be -- going back to this, too, while it's being taken off the screen, from that distance would it be possible to see the house from the main road?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And this next photograph on this scene -- can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an old photograph of the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we may, I have a blown-up photograph that's significantly lightened that we might refer to. If I could put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Do you know who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And do you know when it was taken?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Would you have any guess about it?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was taken around 2001, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why would you guess 2001?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because to the best of my knowledge, that was the first time the investigators entered that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, looking at this photograph, and we have on the ELMO the same photograph, what is the photograph on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph on the ELMO is a copy that I made in my office using a programme called Picasa, which is a -- an addition to the Google programme, and basically all it is is a photo-editing software similar to what you would find in any of -- you know, any of the software packages that are available now.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why did you make that photograph?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was interested to see what the building on the lower left-hand corner of the photograph would reveal. From the photograph that was taken, it's very dark, and you really can't see much detail in that structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What did you see when you lightened the photograph?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a -- it appears to be a garage of some sort that was constructed on part of the Bikavac scene, and you can see the tail of a blue vehicle parked inside that garage, and then it's covered with some sort of a cloth. But what's of interest to me in this photograph is the position of this garage on the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is actually located almost in the centre of the property, and through observation if you'll notice where -- the area where the soldier is standing, you can see where the car has traveled in and out of that garage and has killed all of the vegetation as the vehicle's gone back and forth. There's no growth there, which tells me that that building has been there for some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to see that building when you were at the site visit?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What information do you have about when that building was built?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What information do you have about when that building would have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information on that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what can you tell us as far as an investigator -- investigator's eye goes, when you went to the scene, what did you notice?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the area has been cleaned of this building, obviously, and the -- apparently the neighborhood has continued to use this area as a trash dump. You can see to the soldier's right the beginnings of that pile. I mean, it's got diapers and milk bottles and orange peels and, you know, egg shells and everything. It's just a dump.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Where would the foot-print of the Bikavac house be?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are actually two possibilities to the foot-print of the house, and one of them -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I thought I had the pen on. This line is actually what appears to be a stem wall for some part of a structure, and -- forgive me, this is kind of an odd angle for me to work, but the other part of the stem wall is here, and there's also a stem wall or foundation that runs here, and then a join, if that were a straight line, like that. So maximum size would be to this line; the minimum size would be to this line. The outside wall is here. Approximately 1 metre to the inside, closer to that building, there is a retaining wall that runs here that separates this property from this property. That retaining wall is not even a metre high, but it is -- because of the slope of the hill, in order to level that foundation they had to build a wall, build that up and flatten that area out so that they could construct a level structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: So looking at it from an investigation point of view, what steps should have been taken with this scene?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it really depends on what we decide to do. If the building -- if this building, this garage area is gone, what we want to do, since this is primarily an archaeological dig at this point, we would want to come in, grid this area off, and we would search each one of these quadrants, taking the earth down as far as necessary, and we would be searching for the same things we discussed a moment ago. We'd be looking for hair, bones, documents, anything that would help identify what actually took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does the failure of the investigators to do that in any way affect the reliability of the evidence that would have been presented in relation to that site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the problem is, Your Honour, we don't know what the evidence would have been presented because the evidence has never been collected. If we were talking about simply evidence that had been collected and mishandled, that would be one issue; but the failure to collect the evidence, we have no way of knowing what is there. And again, that speaks directly to whether or not the crime was, number one, committed; and number two, it lacks any evidence to support allegations that are brought forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What could you expect to find if you went there today and performed these site investigations?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is a scene as reported and alleged, I would expect to find some type of human remains there; the reason being, at some point in time this home was cleared, the home -- the lot was cleared off of all the rubble and remains of the fire. But as the Chamber is aware, where a body is consumed in the fire, not necessarily all the body parts are consumed. There is residue and body parts that are left behind. Regardless of how intense the fire is, not all the body parts will burn of all of the victims. So at some point in time, somebody went in and removed the remains of that fire and took the material out to ground level to where we see these stem walls. Over time as it's rained or people have walked on that, the possibility of bone fragments and other evidence would have been pushed into the earth, and I have no evidence to the contrary that a crime scene was taken down below the foundation level, so I have every reason to believe that if the allegations are true, I should find some sort of trace evidence in that soil.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How complicated would it be to undertake a process to examine the soil in that way?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not complicated at all. In fact, that was the work that Dr. Clark was doing back as early as, you know, 1998, 1996. It's really an archaeological dig where you come in, and his particular team, he brought in a pathologist. He brought in an archaeologist. He brought in a forensics expert, and they conducted a search at the two Slap sites north of Visegrad, and they did it by textbook. The site was gridded. The remains were photographed and collected. They collected any evidence that they found, like bullet fragments. All of that was documented and submitted in reports. It was perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- now, you mentioned Dr. Clark, and you mentioned him in your report as well. What does he have to do with these scenes?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has really nothing to do with these scenes, per se, but the work that he did is a classic example of the way that a -- that these scenes should have been worked, and it also indicates to me that they had the technical expertise within a very short distance of Visegrad and probably could have called upon Dr. Clark to assist them in processing the scene if they were unsure how to do it. They had the technical expertise in close proximity fairly early on after the alleged incidents took place in 1992, and they already had the staff, as it were, on the ground. With very little effort, they could have tasked Dr. Clark to come to Visegrad and perform the on-site forensics work at these two scenes, and he would have probably only spent maybe another week, maybe two weeks' time fully excavating that property.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And why wasn't it done in a similar manner at these sites, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And with lack of forensic evidence, what can an investigator look to in these scenes to ultimately find out what happened to the victims?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the forensic evidence or without someone, a witness coming forward and taking the investigator to the site where the remains have been buried, you're really at a loss. There's nothing more you can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What do we know about -- or what do you know, excuse me, about the removal of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about the removal of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Pardon. I need to wait for translation. Why is that important to these investigations?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there's the practical side, the investigative side of the equation, and that is we would want to be able to find and identify the cause of death and the manner of death of these individuals, which is an important part of any homicide investigation. But on the humane, moral side of the equation, I think we owe it not only to the families of the victims but also to the decedents themselves to ensure they receive a proper burial and that the families can deal with their losses properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Where are the remains today?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What is the possibility, given these two fires, and I know that you don't -- you're not a fire expert, but what is the possibility, in your experience in dealing with fire investigations, that the heat was so strong that there were absolutely no remains to be found?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. There has not been any evidence whatsoever either in Mr. Jenkins's report nor in his testimony that he has ever even done a fire investigation. Perhaps we could lay a foundation for his experience, if any, on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What experience have you had in fire investigations directly?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had some limited experience, but it's primarily been to respond -- when I was working as a field investigator, to respond to the fire, and once human remains had been found, to call the arson investigators to the scene. So my experience, really, is casual. I have been on the scene of the fires. I've scene the human remains from various fires, but as far as, you know, any in-depth experience, I really -- I don't have very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of that testimony, I would submit that any evidence relating to this would be excluded from this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. O'Leary would have heard the answer, and I don't think there is much point in putting the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we were just asking hypothetically, based on his experience of being at the scene of fire victims, what he has experienced there, based on his knowledge of what he's seen and knowledge of the fire temperatures and based on the cause what he might expect to find in an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he has described his experience as limited. I think you should move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We can move on, then, Mr. Jenkins, and actually move to the third site of Varda.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen, actually, 1D22-0705, page 13. Again, it's the photo index. Oh, and I apologise. It's my fault. I would like to admit the marked photo that was on the screen, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And actually one thing before we leave Bikavac. If we could go to page 11 of that photo index first, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, you are familiar with the testimony of a survivor of the Bikavac fire?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How did that affect your investigation at the site visit?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a question from an investigative point of view as to whether or not the witness would be able to fit through the opening of the garage door as she has indicated in her various statements. In casual observation of the Visegrad area, I noticed that there were several garage doors that matched the general description of the door described by the witness. And when we got to the Bikavac area, it seems that that particular type of garage door was commonly used among all of the homes that were constructed in that area, and all the homes appear to be fairly contemporaneously constructed. They were all built at approximately the same time, it appears.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: But actually page 11, please, if we could have that on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What's the top photograph, Mr. Jenkins?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photograph of a garage door taken on the -- this building is directly adjacent to the Bikavac fire scene. It is the building that is -- I'm getting my directions -- I think it's to the north of the area, but it is the property that's adjacent -- directly next-door to the Bikavac scene, and this garage door that you see in this photograph is typical of all of the garage doors on the residences in that immediate area.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And when did you take it?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken on 29 January of '09.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What about the photo below it?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That photograph is a measurement showing the height of the door, and unfortunately it's a little bit small, but that door is approximately 5 feet, 5 inches, and all we had was a US standard tape measure. We didn't have a metric measure with us, but it's just over 5 feet tall.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the way, I did the conversion to 165 centimetres after I got home. I didn't have that information with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jenkins. What are these two photographs indicating, if you could start with the top photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph of a measurement from the bottom of the window to the top of the window that you saw in the prior photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And the bottom photograph, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is actually just a close-up of the measurement, and it's 9 inches or approximately 22.9 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why was it important to you to measure the windows?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the witness's statements, she's indicated that she crawled through a window to the ground on the other side where she made her escape, and I have not had the opportunity to visually see the witness, so I felt it was necessary to take these particular photographs to present to the Chamber so that -- since they have seen her, they would be able to assess for themselves whether or not they felt that she could physically fit through that window as she's reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What other possibilities would you entertain with the door besides fitting through the window in her testimony?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it speaks to the injuries, I think, that we have seen on the witness. I've reviewed the photographs that were taken right after the injuries were incurred, and just to refresh the Chamber's recollection, she had severe burns across her forehead, her hair, her left hand. She had lost some fingers due to the fire on her left hand. Obviously, she had been in a severe environment of fire. But the question, then, from a logical standpoint is if she was engulfed in fire inside the house, how much time would it take her to work her way to the window, crawl out of the window on the terrace or through that door, and then make her way through that window? And does that amount of time correspond to the injuries that we see on the witness? So, if you will, she gets to the window, and she starts to climb out. We would expect that it would take a longer period of time for her to work her way through that window and drop out on the other side. That would be fairly quick for her to drop on the other side. But the time it would take for her to climb through that, we would expect the lower torso of this witness to be exposed to the fire for a longer period of time, and I would expect to see more injury on the lower half of her body and on her legs that would also correspond to the injuries that we saw on her head. The lower half of her body would be in the fire for a longer period of time, and I don't believe we have those injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Given the statements that were available to the investigators at the time, what other alternative theories should they have considered, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In her original statements, she had indicated that when she arrived at the police station she told a young soldier that she had tripped -- I believe it was tripped over a butane bottle and had caught her hair on fire, an epileptic fit or something like that. And it seems from the evidence that -- I mean, that is certainly a viable alternative to what happened, and from the injuries that we see on her, that fits more with the evidence that we see on -- the photographic evidence that we see on the witness. From my perspective, it seems that that is a more likely scenario than crawling through that window.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does it affect this investigation that alternative theories weren't pursued, as far as we know?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly could have affected from the very beginning how aggressively the Bikavac fire was investigated. If the possibilities were there that the witness was simply trying to insert herself into an investigation for whatever her motives may be, that option should be considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the other photographs -- I'd like to mark for identification these four photographs of the garage door, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D214, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have 65 ter 175.15 up on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Other than measurement of those garage doors, what type of inspection did you do on those doors? And not referring to the photograph, I was just asking --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, in general?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: -- in general on the garage doors that you saw.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the neighboring door, do you mean? Just general construction of the materials, nothing really specific. We looked at the doors to see, as I indicated earlier, if it appeared to be a common material or a common type of door that was used in that area, and we were drawn to the window simply to -- again, to illustrate the point for the Tribunal so that they could make the assessment in their deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what we have on the screen here now, how does this door, garage door compare to the one that you had seen and photographed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, then, could that type of door like the one you saw be used to block a standard double-wide patio door opening?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it could be. But you would have to -- if you notice, this particular's door is hinged on the side and opens in the middle, so we're really talking about removing both halves of that door in order to block -- if we're talking about a sliding glass door, you would have to remove both halves of that door, which would definitely reduce the ability to secure -- really, at that point we're only talking about half of the mass, half of the volume of the door. You could push half of it over much easier than you could push a one-piece garage door.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what were the doors that you saw made of?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They appear to be made of a lower-grade wood like a -- almost like a plywood.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Would that type of material burn?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, would this height of door, then, completely cover a standard patio opening, door?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it would. It's shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer do you plan to be, Ms. O'Leary?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: I would say half-hour, 45 minutes; 45 minutes, to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can move on to Varda now as I had said before. If we call up -- actually, if we could introduce this photograph, as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could call up P153, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about a site investigation of Varda compared to the two fire scenes?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the scene itself goes, there really is no scene to work. From a forensic side, there's nothing to be done there. The chances of finding any bullet fragments or, you know, to be able to reconstruct anything as far as the scene itself is concerned is non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What is the photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the Varda factory area.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Do you know when it was taken?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Now, as an investigator, if there is not the forensic evidence you're looking for, what should they be looking for in a scene like this?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular scene, I was really calling upon my expertise as a former commander in our narcotics unit where we would plan and execute raids on drug dealers and organised crime operations and trying to put myself in the shoes of someone who was planning a raid on this particular factory; how would I best accomplish that raid with the best chance of success? So if I were to plan an operation where I was going to raid this factory and take some of the employees out, put them under arrest, how would I accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does that relate to surveying this incident scene?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The allegation in Varda is that the defendant drove his vehicle to the area around that small red building that is located in the centre of the photograph, and this -- this building, and then walked in a distance of probably 200 metres or so to the main factory area and took control of several of the employees, then marched them out back to where his car was parked, then down to the river on that -- on this road, and allegedly the employees were then executed down here on the river-bank somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, my interest is in knowing how this impacts on the Prosecution's case because we are not interested in the shortcomings of the investigation. We only have an interest in the shortcomings to the extent that they impact on the credibility, the reliability of the evidence. So I don't want to hear criticisms of the investigation unless they impact on the Prosecution's case. The investigation might have been better. The question is: As good as it was or as bad as it was, has the Prosecution adduced evidence to satisfy the Trial Chamber beyond a reasonable doubt? That's our interest in it. I'm not writing a criticism of the investigation. So each time you ask him a question, I'm waiting to hear how it impacts on the Prosecution's case; otherwise, I'm not going to allow any cross-examination in relation to it because it's not really strictly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: The investigators in this case did take statements that I believe you had access to; yes?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what can you tell me about the distances that you saw on the scene in relation to the statements that were taken?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the distance from the area where the vehicle was parked approximately in here, you can't even see the factory area where the employees were allegedly taken. It is off the photograph back in this area, and the witnesses that were used were located in these houses. So we're talking probably in the area of 200 metres to 220 metres there; I would say a hundred -- somewhere between 75 and a hundred metres here; and probably close to 200 to 225 metres to that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And do you know any indication of the distance between the road and the river-bank?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Down this road?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would estimate that at somewhere in the area of 75 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what about this photograph may be different than at the relevant indicted time-period?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that this retaining wall or this walkway has been constructed since the incident allegedly took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And can I move to admit this photo, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any follow-up investigations in this case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Moving away from forensics, then, I want to talk about how you verify victims. As an investigator, how would you identify murder victims in a case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, there are two ways to identify in a case like this, especially given the time-period. The most reliable way is through DNA, and in the alternative we would be looking either for dental records or possibly unique jewellery or documents of identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If you cannot establish death through forensic materials, what other methodology would you employee as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point -- in this particular instance because we're really talking about a war zone, I think it's imperative that you contact either the Red Cross or the Crescent Moon Society or NATO, some of the organizations that are responsible for moving refugees out of harm's way into a safer location because those organizations are very good at documenting the names of the individuals that they are dealing with. So at a later time, they can put the families back together if they happen to be separated because of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What is the effect if you find later on that some victims are actually not victims of an incident? How does that affect your investigation?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly diminishes the number of decedents that you're concerned with identifying, and I think it would then cause you to even exercise more due diligence as an investigator to ensure that as many people as possible had been identified as being alive and well, and that information then needs to be known -- taken to the families so that they can hopefully reconnect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What does all this have to do with the case? The fault is not yours. Mr. Alarid is rising, as indeed he should. What does all this have to do with the case that we are trying? This is not a university seminar in which we are looking into the short-comings of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be relevant there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am trying a case in which I have to determine the guilt or innocence of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want evidence that will help me in that. This doesn't help me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my jurisdiction, every homicide case is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't care what you do in your jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm turning this case into what I believe is at least addressing some real concerns with regards to the investigation in homicide cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am going to take the adjournment now, and you consult with Ms. O'Leary. If the rest of the examination-in-chief is along those lines, I'm going to stop it. It is not helpful. I have told Ms. O'Leary time and again that the Chamber's only interest in what this very experienced gentleman has to say is if it bores a hole in the Prosecution's case. There's no point telling me that the investigation could have been better, that best practices were not followed. I want to know whether as good as the investigation was or as bad as it was, it doesn't meet the required standards of the Court, and he's not helping us with that. When the trial is finished, you may wish to conduct a seminar into the Prosecution's investigation and excoriate them. That's all well and good, but it is -- frankly it is not -- I do not see it as helping us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I wait to that point, then the benefit to my client is gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no benefit to your client from what I have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, you cannot make a decision in a vacuum. You cannot make a decision in a vacuum. You have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have not seen any benefit. If I were the -- just a minute. If I were the Prosecutor, I would not cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to take the break now, and you must bring this gentleman to shortcomings in the investigation which impact on the Prosecution's case, which tend to make it more unreliable, less credible. I am not interested -- the Chamber is not interested in general principles of investigation. We are not interested in evidence which only shows the shortcomings of the investigation. You may have a sloppy investigation and yet still have enough evidence that proves guilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's perfectly possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and that is why -- that is why it is important for him to tell us how it relates to the evidence, but you have not brought him here to do that. So we take the adjournment now for 20 minutes, and when you come back you see whether we can proceed along a more profitable line for these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have reconsidered the position that I expressed before the break. First, one of my colleagues has reprimanded me for dealing with Ms. O'Leary more severely than Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: If anyone deserves it, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I am reconsidering the position because I see there is another way of looking at the witness's evidence. He is giving evidence about shortcomings in the investigation. It is true that he has not been asked to link it specifically to the Prosecution's case. Maybe he can; maybe he can't. He perhaps doesn't know what that evidence is, but Mr. Alarid can still in his closing submissions allude to this witness's evidence and submit, for example, if there was no DNA, then particular consequences would flow from that. But I would still believe that where he can show how the shortcomings weaken the Prosecution's case, if he has the capacity to do that, that he should do that. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As always, I appreciate your guidance, and I think we can make this pretty brief, almost finished, and try to wrap it all up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, proceeding as the Trial Chamber has discussed, why don't we go scene by scene of the three incidents and sort of tie it all together with your frame of reference as an investigator. Looking at Varda, I know you had the opportunity to look over several witness statements, and you made a site visit. From an investigator's point of view, what shortcomings are there in the investigation that will impact on the Prosecution's case in your mind?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The location of the two female witnesses located on the balconies, if you recall the photograph that was on the screen a few moments ago, the two witnesses that are used are some distance from the scene, and -- pardon me. Could I have the pen? Thank you. And just to refresh everyone's memory since the break, we're talking about the witness in this house and the witness in this house. There is some distance involved here that may or may not be relevant, but certainly with this particular witness, she is looking a considerable distance to try to make identifications of the individuals that are involved in this incident. Same with this lady, although the distances are less. But the fact of the matter is, there were other witnesses that were actually inside the factory at the time that the raid took place and supposedly the gentlemen were arrested and taken out, and that information was apparently discarded in favour of the statements from the witnesses that were further away. As an investigator, I think all of those statements, all of that information should be evaluated and examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How can that make the Prosecution's case more or less reliable?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my perspective it could only make it that much more reliable because you have eyewitnesses inside the factory that actually viewed the events that took place, rather than relying on two casual witnesses that are some distance from the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: When you discuss the statement that was not used or utilised in this case, can you refer to the pseudonym that you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's VG-58, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Are you -- is it --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If the name is easier, I'm not certain, but we would have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And just very briefly, then, in private session, what would be the name of the statement that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the notes in front of me from which to refresh my memory, so I would ask if counsel has any information to help me identify. I don't have the -- I don't remember the VG number of the individual, but I'm aware and remember the incident, but I don't have that documented specifically in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission, I believe we can pull the statement on the screen; otherwise, we can move on to -- however you'd like to proceed on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would object to this statement being brought into evidence in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We don't necessarily need to bring it into evidence, Your Honour. We can just discuss it peripherally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: We can go out of private session, then, if we're not going to discuss any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Without listing the names, then, or any references to which statement it may be, can you tell us what evidence was left out that you feel would have assisted?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identification of the victims, first of all, by name; and secondly, the interaction that took place inside the factory and what that eye-witness saw as far as the actions of the defendant. Those will all be critical to -- to the investigation. I think it would speak directly to the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Do you know where this person would have been located?
