utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was on the factory floor with the coworkers, and I'm not -- I don't know how far or what the distance was. That information was not covered in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And hypothetically speaking, then, as an investigator, if you were to be reviewing this case, this cold case, having the materials that you reviewed with the statements and the site visit and everything that you had available to you, would you hypothetically be referring it to the Prosecution for prosecution?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the overall quality, I would want my investigators to do more before I brought it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on to Bikavac, I believe, now. Same questions and the same recap, basically, of everything that you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. May I ask you, Mr. Jenkins, whether the view that you just expressed would be prompted by your feeling that the evidence would not have been enough to secure a conviction or simply that you yourself would feel more confident with more evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the evidence that was presented is lacking sufficient grounds to warrant conviction, and I would want my investigators to present the Prosecution with the most evidence that we possibly could to ensure that conviction. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: So back to Bikavac. You had the statement and testimony of the survivor, VG-114.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: You had statements and testimony of people who had interacted with her and who had witnessed the alleged incident, and you also had the availability of a site visit.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Putting that all together, what are the shortcomings in that investigation which would impact the OTP's case, in your investigative opinion?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forensics investigation is certainly insufficient. In addition, I think the witness statements required further scrutiny. Their inconsistencies are troubling to me because generally the statements do not match up with the physical evidence that we do have at hand and was present at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Would it assist you if we brought -- [Microphone not activated]. Would it assist you if we brought a map back on the screen in discussing any of this?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can certainly discuss that scene if you wish, in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: I take this opportunity to ask for admission of this marked photograph, then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D217.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And then if we could have -- I believe the aerial of Bikavac is 1D20-0021.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off her microphone when not using it.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, when you're discussing the inconsistencies of witness statements, can you show us on the map what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the inconsistencies as far as the witness statements on Bikavac really deal more with the -- the witness, the survivor. There are more inconsistencies in her statement. However, there are other inconsistencies with another -- another witness and that there's some confusion as to the location where they were actually at when they were witnessing the events. I believe some of the people have identified the area down to the south -- I'm sorry, to the north of that as the scene, and that's led to some confusion as to what they actually saw, as well as we have never really been able to -- or I have been unable to identify with any surety the property from which VG-114 was removed and taken to the scene. There are some other issues that I have concerning how they collected all the alleged victims from the residences in that immediate area and why the witnesses themselves were not taken to the scene and executed. If they're having a general round-up of all of the Muslims in that particular area and performing a summary execution, then why was this house with several witnesses left behind when it is in close proximity to the scene? I mean, these are all questions that I have as to why that took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. How does this -- these shortcomings as you've just described now affect the Prosecution's case in reliability?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my mind, it affects the Prosecution's case because we really don't have a firm idea of what happened. There are too many variables, too many loose ends in the investigation. There are too many other possible alternative answers that we have not sorted through and come up with a conclusion as to the most likely cause of the events. There's just too many loose ends.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What specifically -- which loose ends would you like to wrap up in investigating?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which what?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Which loose ends that you just referred to would you be looking to shore up?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we should talk more with 114 and find out exactly what happened. She finally gave her testimony before the Tribunal, and I understand that that is the final record as to the events, but that testimony needs to be weighed against the physical evidence that we've brought today concerning the door. In addition -- and that sort of stuff should have been addressed in advance. We should have the answers to those questions months ago, even years ago, rather than at the 11th hour in front of the Tribunal. We should have known all of that stuff. In addition, the credibility of other witnesses that were in close proximity to the fire and the identification of individuals; for example, the photo boards that were used, the fact that according to the witnesses all of the offenders at the scene were either wearing balaclavas or ski masks and yet the witnesses were asked to identify the alleged offenders off a photo board, rather than using a voice identification which would be a more proper way to identify people. The witness says she is familiar enough with Mr. Lukic's voice that she would know him anywhere, and yet she wasn't given the opportunity to identify him by his voice. Rather, she was just given a photo array, and she allegedly has known this man for years and years. In my mind that, negates the photo board. That entire identification process was merely an attempt to bolster the investigation, the credibility of the case, but was done so improperly.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does the method taking of statements, of -- being interviewed and digesting differ from in -- a question and answer in this case? How does it affect this specific incident?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the transcript that we have before us. It is a record, word by word, of my testimony and the questions that have been asked. By taking a statement in that manner, the investigators really have an advantage because they can pour through those testimonies much the same as the Tribunal is going to do when they evaluate our testimony, and they're going to find nuances in that statement that otherwise may be lost, number one. Number two, there's a possibility of misinformation being either translated because of regional dialect or because of a misunderstanding between the translator and the witness. By providing a tape statement, similar to the transcript that we have before us, that translation can later be retranslated if necessary, and the transcripts can be compared side by side to make sure that everything is transcribed or has been translated properly. It also gives not only the Prosecution the opportunity to have a complete record of what the witness has said, but at a later time it also gives the opportunity to the Defence to do the same thing, so it equals -- it levels the playing field for both sides. With the system that they're using with an interview being conducted and a statement being taken or prepared by the investigator and then being sworn to by the witness, there's a tremendous amount of opportunity for lost information, and also, the investigator has the opportunity to insert his own bias into the investigation. And many of the witnesses do not have the education or the ability to recognise that they possibly are being manipulated and are then willing to sign the statement, trusting that the investigator knows what he's doing and is doing everything properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: So, again, I'd ask you, Mr. Jenkins, in regard to Bikavac, hypothetically speaking, if you were reviewing this cold case with the materials that you had available, the site visit, would you feel comfortable referring it to the Prosecution for further trial?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there's too many inconsistencies in the statements, which I think could have been rectified had statements been taken with the other format. There's too much inconsistency with the evidence. Her injuries do not, in my mind, coincide with the events that have been described by the witness, and the credibility of some of the witnesses that were in close proximity to the events, what they saw, who they identified, are in question. And the other individuals, the other witnesses that were being detained in the house had no direct sight or direct knowledge of the event but, rather, are relying on hearsay information from the information of VG-114.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could move on, then, finally, to Pionirska. Again, you've reviewed the statements of several of the witnesses, survivors. You've had opportunity to take a site visit.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Exactly what shortcomings in the investigation do you believe, as an investigator, would impact the OTP's case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the lack of forensic evidence as we've already discussed at length. Secondly, the location of VG-114. She was not in a position to observe anything other than ambient light. Third, the testimony from the witness that managed to escape the march from the residence above the Pionirska scene. She and her sister ducked into the area behind a shed and escaped the area. She said that she had heard gun-shots and heard screaming up to an hour after the incident took place before she manage to work her way out of the scene. In my mind, that is inconsistent with the evidence -- or with the theory that's presented by the Prosecution concerning the fire. That room in the basement of Pionirska would be like an oven. If there was an accelerant used in that room, the temperatures would have risen tremendously. It would have been very, very hot in there, and within a matter of a few moments, the lung tissue of the people in that room would have cooked, and they would have died probably within 5 or 10 minutes maximum. So the idea that people were alive in that room for an hour does not fit the evidence or the theory that I see as being put forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What impact does it have that the witnesses and the alleged survivors identified a person or persons who were later found not to be there?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It speaks to the credibility of the witnesses and exactly what they saw. Then the question is, what is their motive?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And how overall does your investigation of the case and looking at the files, what have you found that makes the Prosecution's case more or less reliable?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really a repeat of everything that we've already testified to from the forensics side of the case through the way the statements were taken to the crime scenes. I mean, there's so many areas of this investigation that are lacking in specificity, and we have no reports from the investigators to give us any information as to why they did the things they did. If you recall yesterday, I am a Prosecution-oriented individual. I have spent, you know, my 23 years on the Albuquerque Police Department putting people in gaol and providing my Prosecution team with the best possible cases that I could. I am surprised, I guess, at the quality of the work that was presented to the Prosecution, the lack of reports. We have no way of knowing, either side, what was done or why, and I am sensitive to the fact, Your Honours, that it was a war zone, but at some point in time it was secure enough that these investigations and -- these investigations could have been carried out in a safe manner, even if it required taking in a small security team. The evidence that potentially was lost certainly outweighs the risk of not obtaining the evidence. You know, Dr. Clark was in in 1996 collecting evidence from the Slap scenes. I don't see why the evidence couldn't have been collected as early as 1996 in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question, then, about Pionirska, again, hypothetically, as an investigator having the materials that you had to review, would you feel comfortable referring it to a Prosecution for further case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with the evidence I have before me now, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, with your indulgence, I found the statement for Varda, actually, of the person who he had been referring to. If we could pull it up on the screen and see if that somehow helps. I know the Prosecution had an objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just to renew the objection, Your Honours. This witness is not someone who testified. It's an out-of-court statement from an out-of-court declarant not tested in court, and there's no -- this is a -- it seems to me an inadmissible way to try and get this in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: May I? And I don't mean to interrupt, but this is important, Your Honour, and they've used the ability to hide this witness from us in not calling them as a position, and this investigator reviewed a statement, that is why he gave the opinion, and I think it's important that you see the statement. This was in the Prosecution's control. It was within their purview, and they made a strategic decision not to call this witness. It is highly relevant to the investigation if you consider the claims about Varda and the testimony of the witnesses. This witness within the factory directly disputes the eyewitnesses that have appeared before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution strongly objects to Mr. Alarid's representation of this as being hidden. It was disclosed to the Defence on the 22nd of August of 2008. It was certainly not hidden, and they have had it in their possession. They could have listed this witness as a Defence witness if they found it was relevant. They chose not to do so, and this is not the proper way to get it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid apologises for the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did list him as a Defence witness, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. From the perspective, though, it is funny that ICTY statements involving an indictment count come to us after trial started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I already apologised on your behalf, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, this is not an ICTY statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's understanding is that this statement was utilised by the witness in his work and assisted him in his conclusions. We believe the statement can be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could call up 1D22-0049. I believe it's redacted, but just for safe measure, maybe not show it to the public gallery. Yes, it's a totally redacted statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, there's a document on your screen. Is this document familiar to you, and we can move through other pages if it assists.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be the cover sheet for the statement of VG-31.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What significance does that have to you?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: VG-31 was one of the statements that I reviewed as part of my assessment of the Varda file.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If we could go to the third page of the statement, I believe. Oh, I'm sorry, the [microphone not activated]. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What specifically in this statement that you reviewed would you have liked to have -- or would you have presented to the Prosecutor as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did we want to go to page 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Two. Two has come up here. Or why specifically did you mention -- if I rephrase, maybe it's easier. Why specifically did you mention this individual and his vantage point?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was actually on site in the factory and was in a position to see what was going on, and his vantage point was much better than the witnesses that had been presented.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How many statements did you review of this witness?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just reviewed the one, this particular statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Just this particular statement?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Are you certain?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Is this the four-page statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: There's only three pages on this statement, Mr. Jenkins.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one I reviewed I believe was four pages long, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If we could put 1D22-0045 on the screen, please, then. And again, this one is not redacted, so please don't broadcast to the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: On the right side of your screen -- well, in the centre of your screen now, what can you tell me about this statement in relation to your material review?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can you magnify that one more time? Thank you. Concerning this particular statement? Can we move down -- thank you. So page 1 really deals with the conversation that took place between the witness and other parties that were involved in -- or other parties that were there, and at that point the report is made that the paramilitary group is there and it is taking people.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Of course. But relevant to Varda, what part --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Relevant to Varda, what part of this statement made you mention it?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What really got me was the fact that -- number one, the way they burst in. He uses the term "burst in," which indicates to me that it's more of a raid situation than just casually walking in. That would speak to me of the tactics that were used to gain entry into the factory, and the inconsistency, then, why would you park your car 200 metres away, walk casually up to the factory, and then burst in. If you're going to conduct any kind of a raid, especially if you are as important as the Prosecution alludes to the defendant, you would just drive your car right up to the door and get out and execute the raid. That was inconsistent for me. Also, if we can go down to the -- I guess to the next page. He talks about -- at this point how the body -- or how the individuals were taken out, and allegedly taken down to the area and shot. And he states then that as he left the scene, he saw the bodies in the river and were supposedly later excavated as part of the Slap find. I'm not sure how he knows that information, and it's -- the record from the investigators is moot on that point. We don't know how he got there to that conclusion. But he is able to identify by name the individuals that were taken from the scene at Varda and allegedly executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And in doing so, how was Milan Lukic involved?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Supposedly, Milan Lukic was the individual that was conducting the raid and was responsible for marching these people down to the river-bank for execution.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How does this testimony that we've seen in these two statements -- not testimony, excuse me. How do these statements affect the Prosecution's case in Varda?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it puts an eye-witness in the scenario where he can identify the individuals that were allegedly taken and killed versus simply just having two women on a balcony over a hundred metres away that can make no identification at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jenkins. It seems the question presumes that Mr. Jenkins had reviewed two statements, whereas if I understood it correctly, he's only reviewed this one statement from the Bosnian authorities, not the ICTY statement, if I understood Mr. Jenkins correctly. I think counsel tried to show him the first statement. He said it was actually a four-page statement, I think, that he had reviewed, and then you called this one up and this was the one that he recognised. So if I'm correct with that, then it would be only with regard to this statement from the Bosnian authorities that he's speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the other statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jenkins, for -- thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have a question. I missed something, I think, but why didn't the Defence of Milan Lukic call VG-31? Was there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is that VG-31, he was on the original list that we had had, which was quite comprehensive, but due to cutting down, he was one that had been taken off the lists at some point. Oh, I believe it was because he was a part of the communications about contact information, and in the end we were never able to secure contact information for this gentleman. Thank you. And Your Honour, I would move to admit just the second Bosnian statement, then, the second one that he had said he had reviewed as a part of his materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object to it being admitted for the purpose of the proof of the matter asserted in the statement. It's been completely untested. It's an out-of-court statement of another declarant. For it to be used explicitly as a basis for assessing Mr. Jenkins's evidence, I think that probably the foundation for that has been laid, but as to the truth of what is internally in it, we would object to it being used for that particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have anything on that, Ms. O'Leary?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the total of the contents of the statement actually go to why it would affect the credibility of the Prosecution's case in this investigation. As an investigator, he said he would have included it and he would have made sure that this was an integral part -- I'm using words that were not his, so excuse me. But he would have included it as part of his investigation, and as a vital part, I believe that then the substance does go to the fact of what he has reviewed and how it affects the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, but Your Honours, what we're saying is simply that in the context of Mr. Jenkins's evidence, for example, when Defence makes closing submissions, they can feel free to say that Mr. Jenkins assessed this as relevant evidence for the following reasons. That's part of his evidence. But if the Defence is going to base their closing arguments as to the Varda incident on information contained in here, this would be an improper method to get this statement in. There are rules for -- rules which we use to get in witness statements, and this does not fall under one of those. So it's just about the way that it's used that I would object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are those rules?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Well, they can call the witness. I think they can still call the witness, or they can try through 92 quater or a 92 bis motion if -- there are rules under 92 bis and quater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We reserve on the admissibility of the statement. Please proceed. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Just one more question from that statement, then. How in any way does it implicate other suspects in the Varda crime?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're named. There are other suspects in there that certainly should be examined more closely as being involved in the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And how does that impact the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it impacts it tremendously in helping them to sort out exactly what happened at this particular scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jenkins. We have just one more area before we're finished here, very brief. I'd briefly like to talk about arrest warrants and identifying suspects. In your jurisdiction, can you put out an arrest warrant?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: How do you do that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a preparation of an affidavit stating the reason why there's probable cause to believe that an individual has committed a crime. That affidavit is then taken along with the arrest warrant before a judge. It is sworn to as far as the truth and veracity of the affidavit, and if the judge is satisfied that the affidavit is true and correct, a warrant would be issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And have you ever dealt in your time as an officer, investigator, and deputy chief, have you ever dealt with an out-of-state or international warrant?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: In those cases, what measures do you take to ensure that you have the right person if you find the suspect?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally on the warrant there are descriptors that would help me identify to ensure that the individual that we have in custody is in fact the same person that's listed on the warrant, the purpose being to eliminate individuals that have the same or similar names.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And if we could have 1D22-0494 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this, Ms. O'Leary?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're calling on the screen actually the warrant for Mr. Milan Lukic's arrest. I have about five questions for the gentleman about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but still I have to ask what is that you intend to show by the warrant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: May I? Your Honour, the bottom line is that if you look at the statements given by the witnesses that have been presented by the Prosecution, there were some early identifying markers. It is our theory of the case that some of those witnesses were used to compile the description that ultimately led to Mr. Lukic's arrest in Argentina. Those physical descriptions came from, we think, like I said, a compilation of descriptions that have appeared before the Court and are already part of the record. And based on that fact, the warrant, we believe, empirically and on its face, is not an accurate description of the man sitting in court today. So by reference, you've got to infer that doubt, if you will, that the people that identified a person who committed a crime, when the description of that person so is differential from the actual description, it brings into doubt, that reasonable doubt that the person identified at the crimes is in fact the person, Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But we have had evidence from witnesses who knew the accused before --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and who identified -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- and for instance, VG-63 noted Mr. Milan Lukic as having double eagle tattoos. On that warrant are double eagle tattoos. Another VG witness indicated blue eyes. On that warrant is blue eyes, and a mole above the lip. So from the standpoint of the evidence and the basic appearance of the gentleman in court, we believe that those people correctly identified who they believe committed the crime, but if that warrant does not fit the description of the suspect, as an investigator he has a duty, and that's what we're here to explore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You lost me. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly. It seems that it's been put to the witnesses; the witnesses who describe moles, it was put to them; the witnesses that describe blue eyes, it was put to them. To now at this late stage take a document that is compiled from a number of unknown sources, I don't see what relevance it has. Mr. Lukic is going to testify next week. He can tell us the colour of his eyes. He can tell us what tattoos he has, and it'll be for the Chamber to consider that in light of the descriptions given by the witnesses. But to ask Mr. Jenkins about his views about a warrant when neither Mr. Jenkins or any of us in the courtroom know the providence or the source of any of the descriptions contained in the warrant I suggest has absolutely no relevance in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the relevance is, Your Honour, on the face of the warrant the applicant for the warrant is the ICTY, one; secondly, within the purview of the warrant, we requested the records of Milan Lukic from Interpol. Conveniently or coincidentally, the Interpol file on Milan Lukic in Bosnia was lost, and so we were unable to get the verifying file, if you will, that Interpol should have kept for purposes of the warrant and description. But I think it's very suspect that the OTP would make an attempt to exclude a warrant for which they applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary, the Chamber will not allow this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Without the document, then, I have just a couple questions on that matter that are similarly related.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Have you ever met Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: When did you meet Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What was the occasion of that visit?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the detention facility here in The Hague and had a visual examination of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: When you say visual examination, can you explain what you were visualising, which ...

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for identifying marks that are described on the document and trying to see if in fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jenkins. Your Honours, can we know which document Mr. Jenkins is referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the warrant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Without referring to the warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is really difficult to dance around something that shouldn't be danced around. I believe a warrant is a self-authenticating document. It exists within the court system for the benefit of both the Court, the investigators, and the arresting officers. The fact that we're dancing around it is something that an investigator and an officer would regularly review and incorporate when you arrest a suspect is the description within the warrant. The proffer that we are making is, Your Honour, is that the warrant was reviewed by the officer as if he were the investigating and arresting officer, and he in fact conducted an inspection of the suspect as to confirmation or exclusion by virtue of the warrant description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is to be gathered from this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: This is an identification case, Your Honour. It is our theory of the case that the person -- if these people were in fact victimized yet hardly knew Milan Lukic, isn't there a shred of possibility that by virtue of cross-referencing a name to an erroneous description that they in fact could believe a Milan Lukic was the perpetrator, and in fact it wasn't. If they gave the description based on that belief of a blond hair, blue-eyed person, or a gentleman with tattoos, then that goes to the weight of that identification evidence. This is an ID case. We are not by any way stipulating, and the fact that we've presented alibi evidence goes to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would make just one brief point on that. If Mr. Jenkins has reviewed all the witness evidence as to identification, I'm still not clear on what the relevance is of the arrest warrant. If he wants to talk about his observations of the physical description compared to the witness evidence he reviewed with specific reference to particular evidence, then it seems fine. I still don't think the warrant is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Consistent with the ruling we gave earlier, we will not allow any evidence relating to the warrant.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Not mentioning the warrant, leaving that out of this, when you met with Milan Lukic, please explain the purpose of the visit or what visual review you did.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I met Mr. Lukic was inside the facility, as I said, here at The Hague, and I asked Mr. Lukic if he wouldn't mind stripping to the waist, and he complied willingly, and I conducted a visual examination of Mr. Lukic, looking on both arms, under his arms, checking his torso, checking his face, his neck, all of his upper body.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what colour was his hair?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dark brown.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what colour were his eyes?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dark brown as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What tattoos did he have that were visible to you on his upper torso and/or head?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no tattoos at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What evidence is there of any tattoos previously being there that may have been removed or altered?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no evidence of ever having had tattoos. The skin is soft and there's no scarring on anything on either of the arms that would tend to make me think that at one point there had been tattoos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have experience in that area, Mr. Jenkins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have experience in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of examining bodies? Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, of saying whether a tattoo might have been present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen tattoo removal on many prisoners over the years, and I am familiar with the scarring that takes place when those tattoos are removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and you saw none.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What birth-marks did you see from the head?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no birth-marks. Especially on his face, there are no moles or birth-marks or anything like that on his face.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: What about on his torso, arms?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several small moles on his back, but they're not birth-marks. They're just -- they're small moles.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And what, if any, other identifying features are there that would be remarkable?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is approximately, I believe, 186 centimetres versus the height on the warrant which is 183 --

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Please don't reference the warrant.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. But he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much in feet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say he's about 6'1", 6 feet 1. Medium build, appears to be in good shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you speak to the question of any moles that might have been on his face which might have been removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not -- I did not see anything that appeared to be a surgery. There is a small spot on the lip, but not being a physician I could not say what that is, but there was no indication of a mole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: And what if any scars were you able to ascertain?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no scars at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all the questions I have right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, my name is Maxine Marcus, and I'm going to be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you are clearly a very highly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I neglected to tell Ms. Marcus that she performed commendably in marshalling --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary. I think you mean Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary. I think Ms. Marcus doesn't need a commendation.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You can commend Ms. Marcus after she's finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the comments that I made, I think you marshalled the evidence commendably.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: No, and thank you for the guidance. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, you're clearly a very highly experienced police officer, and we're honored to have you here. Am I correct in understanding that your law enforcement experience has been exclusively carried out in Albuquerque, New Mexico?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you clarify for us, please.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a former reserve agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. Also at one time, I was part of a drug enforce -- the USDEA Task Force, and we therefore had national jurisdiction. And we have investigated and been involved in large-scale money laundering operation involving a former attorney general for the state of New Mexico who was laundering money through the state of Kentucky into China, into South America, and then into the Caribbean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. So could you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please remember to pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, then, how much time, in years or -- that you spent with the Air Force and with the USDEA Task Force.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time with the Air Force I really need to break into two sections, if that's okay with you, because part of it was as a munitions technician in my first enlistment with the air guard, and I was recruited, then, to go into OSI as a reservist because of my experience with the police department. So my actual time in OSI is about 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us what years those were?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in OSI from 1976 through 19 -- let's see. So it would have been, I'm sorry, 1974 through approximately 1986.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now could I ask the court officer, please, to call up, please, 1D208 and just to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, while we're calling that up, it was a little bit difficult to figure out from your CV exactly how many years you spent in each role. You described a wide variety of responsibilities, but the years were not indicated.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So can you tell us, how long were your tenure as the deputy chief of police of the Albuquerque Police Department?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what years were those, please?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left in January of 1996, so 1994 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at your -- the front page of your CV, it says that your work history relating to the Albuquerque Police Department was from 1972 to 2008. So is that an error, or did we misunderstand something there?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that -- that is a work history from 1972 to 2008. That is not necessarily within APD, but 2008 was when the CV was prepared, so that would probably be a little bit misleading on my part to you, and I will correct that. Thank you for bringing that to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No problem. So when you testified yesterday that you began this company that you set up, Jenkins and Jenkins, that was after your retirement from the APD. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, as -- in your role, in your two-year role as the deputy chief of the APD, you were responsible for all aspects -- you were responsible for aspects outside law enforcement. That's what you told us yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Areas outside of direct law enforcement responsibilities. Basically the administrative aspects of the organisation, the day-to-day operation, the budgetary, communications, those sorts of things, rather than responsibility for investigators or officers making arrests and investigating crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now I'm pausing just for the -- so you know, for the transcript. Now, so I presume in that role you had input into the hiring, firing, and promotion of police officers in the APD. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing to do with promotion. That is done through an outside agency through an assessment centre process, but hiring -- I'm sorry, but internal affairs deals with the disciplinary aspects of it. And we do hire through personnel through testing and psychological profiling, and at that point they come before what is called the chief selection committee, which I chaired, and then we make a final determination whether or not we will tender an offer for employment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So to review the number of years of investigative experience specifically, I'm just going to break it up. How many years of your, I think, 24 years in total of service, approximately --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Twenty-three. Now, how many years did you spend directly engaged yourself in carrying out criminal investigations in the field?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a supervisor but as a --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Directly carrying it. I'm going to break it out in that way.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I think that in last couple of weeks my main activity in this courtroom is just interrupting for translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry that you have been confined to the rule, Mr. Cepic, but I'm going to ask the witness and the Prosecutor to observe the pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's not that usual, Mr. Jenkins, that we question somebody in our own language speaking English, so it's -- it's a temptation.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, and I will try to do my part as well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, please, observe the pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you were describing to us, I think, the number of years you spent directly engaged in criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- if you're talking solely about detective work, is that what you're referring to? Because criminal investigations are also conducted by officers in the field on lower-level crimes, so if you're talking about specific time in detectives, that will be different. And I just want to make sure that I can answer your question correctly so that you're satisfied with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at is that I think your evidence yesterday included some roles that you served in the crime lab and some other roles that you served in supervising investigations, so I'm trying to break it out how many years in the field conducting investigations. If a detective is doing that, as well, I'd like to know about that. So actual field investigations into criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That would probably with that caveat begin with my role as a field investigator, which would have been 1976, I believe. That is when you actually begin, in my case, doing the forensics aspects of it, which would be part of the criminal investigation process. From there, I went into the burglary and narcotics unit where I served six years, so that's a total of eight there. Came back to burglary for about another six or eight months after my temporary assignment to the planning and research division -- department. At that time, I got promoted to the rank of sergeant, and I went to the field as a field supervisor, so I was not involved at that time with investigations per se but, rather, supervising officers in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, Judge Van Den Wyngaert is asking me, do we need all of this? I know it -- probably you will say it goes to the weight that we'll attach to his evidence as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I intended it to be rather brief. I think the detail is probably unnecessary. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, sir, so how many years in your law enforcement career did you spend in internal investigations?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not spend any time in internal investigations. They reported to me as a deputy chief, so I'm in their chain of command but did not function as an investigator in internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So if they reported to you, did that mean that you had an active role in managing the investigation or you were in the chain of command and received the information that they produced?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. I'm in a chain of command. That information was reviewed by me, and if the investigation crossed my desk and I felt more investigation needed to be done, then the investigation was sent back down with a note.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in which of these roles, and again, we are trying to be a little bit brief, if possible, an approximate number is fine. In which of these roles did you gain experience conducting interviews with victims of serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily my role in violent crimes. As the supervisor in the sex crimes unit, I only had four investigators working with me at that time and was involved in the interview process with many of the victims and the offenders, not only of sex crimes but also of homicides.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So could you estimate for us approximately how many cases you dealt with which involved interviewing victims of serious crimes. An approximate number will be fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well over a hundred. Well over a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in how many of those interviews did you use an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe five, six.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And have you ever investigated a cold case?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And how many cold cases have you investigated?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say in the area of 15 or 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Have you ever conducted a protracted investigation after the commission of a crime, so now I'm differentiating between surveillance and tracking in narcotics cases which can be protracted and money laundering, but after the commission of a violent crime, a protracted investigation, have you ever done that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And how many approximately of those have you conducted, sir?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two that I can think of right off the top of my head that involved a serial rapist. Those investigations, one was approximately 18 months and the other one was almost three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, the APD has faced a wide variety of internal challenges over the years. Would you say that statement is accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As any other police department.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll return to that a little bit later. Now, the international crimes you referred to yesterday in terms of international investigations, those are primarily money laundering; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Money laundering and drug trafficking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the international part of that, can you clarify for us, what's the international part of that type of an investigation? Bank transfers or -- for money laundering is -- with foreign banks, is that where the international component comes in?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes. The case involved -- the money laundering aspects were these: We were to give the contact in New Mexico a specific amount of money, whatever that might be. The money was then taken or transferred from the offender's bank in Albuquerque to a bank in Louisville, Kentucky, and was deposited in a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't need to hear about his money laundering experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Maybe I could -- I don't mean to interrupt you but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I just wanted to know if that was the international part of his criminal investigative work, so I think I received generally a yes answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's certainly part of it, but we also did extensive investigations on narcotics side, the smuggling aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, would it be accurate to say that you have never investigated violations of international criminal law?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you never received any specified training in investigating international criminal law violations; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you've never conducted or been involved in any investigations during an armed conflict or immediately after the armed conflict; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, I'd like to turn to a few of the aspects of your testimony earlier and just ask you a few follow-up questions. You gave us some evidence in relation to VG-115 and the Pionirska incident, and you talked about the view she had and we had some input from Judge Van Den Wyngaert about the angle and what she said she saw and what she didn't see. Now, in your side bar that you attached, your addendum, you attached a number of different photos with different perspectives from near VG-115's location, so an alley and on the streets, and other angles were included. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, all those other photos, apart from the one photo which was taken exactly from the angle where VG-115 said she was standing, those other photos are quite irrelevant to the case; isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How would you say that they're relevant?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I think they allow you to put into context the surroundings that she saw other than just standing from the balcony looking out. You have to have some idea in context of the surroundings. So I don't think they were irrelevant [Realtime transcript read in error "relevant"] at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: But if I understood your testimony, your suggestion was that from her perspective she couldn't have seen the actual house that was burning, from her perspective. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you questioned that aspect of her evidence.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So the angles from other places, other than where she was standing, would not be relevant to a question about the veracity of her evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you feel you've explained it before, but if you have something else to add as to why the other angles would be helpful --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just before he does that, if you look at -- it's 76, line 5: "So I don't think they were relevant at all." I believe the witness said "irrelevant," if I was not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I believe they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You believe they are relevant, so it should be: "I don't believe they were irrelevant at all."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Please continue your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think by, for example, the one photograph that is taken further up the street that shows the balcony and the house -- and the house that's immediately adjacent to the location of VG-115, it gives you some perspective on the overall view that she had versus simply standing on the balcony and taking a picture. In order to really understand what the surroundings were and what she had the opportunity to see, you need to have a much broader view of the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the Bikavac incident, hypothetically speaking, if there was evidence that the metal door was perhaps on its side, or if there were some other evidence as to the metal door, would you perhaps reconsider your assessment of the climbing, et cetera, that you gave?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am always open to new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if the witness testified that actually she escaped through a space, and if she gave evidence that the space in her estimation was approximately 60 centimetres, would that evidence also impact on your assessment of her evidence?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I actually saw that in her statements, but it was one of the things that's -- the story bounces back and forth and without any reports from the investigators to try to make sense of exactly what happened, it's difficult to tell. But certainly, if that information is the true story, the correct story, that certainly could have some impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the Varda incident, the witness whose evidence you discussed, who you suggested the Prosecution may have wished to call, that witness was describing an incident prior to the charged incident. Would you say that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, I believe, contemporaneous. There were some instances before the incident, but it was kind of a description of what happened from a time immediately before the incident through the finding of the bodies in the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. If I understood your evidence on that point correctly, there were essentially three aspects of the evidence that that witness's statement made you think about. Just to group them - and tell me if I'm inaccurate, please - the first one was essentially the raid, the evidence of a raid; second was the question of the identity of the victims; and the third was the possibility of other perpetrators. Would you say that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the raid, you said that a raid would not be conducted in the way that was described this way, that a raid would not be conducted by parking 200 metres away. So the terminology of the word "raid" was not accurate. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that's jargon-ish, if that's a word, but from my perspective as a career law enforcement officer, if I were the defendant, I would drive to the door of the factory, get out of my car, and walk three steps into the factory rather than park my car 200 metres away and run the risk of being seen and have all of the people that I wanted to arrest flee from the scene. The further away you park, you lose that aspect of surprise. So if you're really -- if you're really trying to catch somebody, you want to catch them in as short amount of time as possible rather than give them the opportunity to flee, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Now, the witness didn't actually use the word "raid." The witness used the word "burst in," right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So if my son bursts into my room, you're interpreting that -- you know, bursting in could mean a variety of things; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hopefully it's not a raid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. Now, you saw other evidence relating to the Varda factory, as well, and so I presume that you saw that there were other witnesses who testified to the identification of the victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And in addition to that, there is another witness who did testify, whose statements I'm sure you reviewed, who was also similarly inside the factory, but instead of seeing an incident prior to the charged incident, she actually saw the incident that was charged.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, based on your assessment, then, of VG-31's statement, which, by the way, was a statement to the Bosnian authorities and not a Tribunal statement, VG-31 talks about some other perpetrators, but the way it's written it could read that those were perpetrators who appeared in the factory before the charged incident. Would you say that's accurate? In other words, there could have been other perpetrators who visited the factory on that day, but because of the time-frame, because VG-31 says in that statement or the statement apparently reads that VG-31 left and then came back even after those other perpetrators were there, and when he came back, he then heard that the machines had been shut off and some of the factory workers had been taken out.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that that's a possibility, but, again, going back to -- and I hate to go back to the work of the investigators, but that could have all been cleared up and made much clearer rather than the different statements being so inconsistent. I would much rather have seen all of those statements clarified in such a way that these questions could have been answered up front. But in answer to your question specifically, there is some difference, I think, between the statements of the two witnesses. Does that answer your question, or did I confuse you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No. So which two witnesses now are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the witness that we were discussing earlier --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I believe it was the one that was in the office area, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you didn't see the ICTY statement taken from VG-31, did you? You testified earlier when it was brought up that you hadn't -- you hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the three-page document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. No, I had not seen that three-page document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you don't actually know whether VG-31 may have clarified something that was in the statement taken by the Bosnian police in the interview with the ICTY investigators.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, the APD has standard operating procedures in place, I'm sure, like any police department which govern your law enforcement activities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You say in your report on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: What's the APD, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The Albuquerque Police Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You say in your report on page 8 as follows: "With a time differential of two to four years after the incidents, the opportunity to collect residue from explosive matter, accelerants, and other time-sensitive evidentiary items was lost when the investigators failed to do their due diligence at the scene. The technical ability to collect these items was in use world-wide in the time-frame from 1992 to 1994." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you also testified yesterday that: "If you leave the scene before the scene is processed, it's generally considered from that point forward that the scene has been abandoned, and any evidence that is obtained subsequent to the time that the scene has been released is of no value." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in your jurisdiction, I presume that when a crime takes place, one of the first things an investigator under your command would do is to secure the area. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In fact, you described to us some of the steps, so I'm not going to go through them at length, but basically, if I understood you correctly, the investigator would observe the scene, photography, maybe draw some sketches of the scene thereafter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And then you might advise the investigators under your command to measure the room or the scene and thereafter take a visual inventory of the evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, while this is going on or immediately following this, your investigators would identify victims and eye-witnesses and seek to interview them, I presume.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And in your jurisdiction, each and every one of those interviews is tape-recorded or simultaneously transcribed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're tape-recorded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So just to be clear, every interview with any witness - I'm not talking about suspects now - any witness that's done by APD officers is tape-recorded and thereafter transcribed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to what all officers at APD do. I can only speak to my experience, and the experience is that is not necessarily the case, but then again, we are not investigating a war crime with such magnitude where it is essential that all of this information be made available to both sides. The gravity of the crime, even though homicide is so -- it's a terrible thing, but in this particular instance we're talking about a situation that is very explosive and the necessity for both sides to have a fair and equal hearing and provide testimony before the Tribunal outweighs any other considerations. And it just seems to me that given that gravity those interviews should be tape -recorded and transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you're suggesting that this investigation in this context, every interview should have been tape-recorded and transcribed, but actually in your practice back home, that may or may not be actually done. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the circumstances, it may vary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And during your time as deputy chief, were all witness interviews for serious crimes tape-recorded and transcribed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak because investigations were not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. And so then in the standard operating procedures, let's say, of the APD, is there a provision which requires all witnesses who are -- all interviews of witnesses of serious crimes to be tape-recorded and transcribed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no standard operating procedure to that effect. However, in instances, for example, in internal affairs investigations, because of the gravity concerning the allegations of misconduct, of police misconduct, those interviews are tape-recorded and transcribed and made part of the record for the very reasons that I've described here. It is a matter of propriety and the appearance of propriety to the community.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And how about in homicide cases?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Homicide cases, again, it depends. If you're dealing with someone that is speaking a second language, I would require my investigators to tape those and have them transcribed because it's a second language.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So I think you said that you did interviews with an interpreter five times in your career; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And those -- those were audio-taped and transcribed?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I suppose -- going back to the order in which you would investigate a crime scene, I suppose that the victims or eye-witnesses might be re-interviewed over time as the evidence is built, is gathered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. It depends on the circumstance. What we would prefer to do, I think, is to allow the witness the opportunity to make the best possible statement they could the first time so that the information is fully documented and not have to go back and repeatedly interview witnesses. I would much rather have a statement from a witness that is more contemporaneous with the events, while the memory is still fresh, rather than a statement that is taken 10 or 15 years down the road, where the memory has failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take the break now. Before we break, can you tell me how long you'll be, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would estimate about an hour and a half. I'll try to make it less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the absence of Judge Van Den Wyngaert, Judge David and I sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Ms. Marcus, to pick up the pace.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, over the break I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is just complete the evidence at this session, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'll do my very best.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Jenkins, at the break I was informed by the interpreters that in spite of the warnings, we have not heeded them, so I'll try and do my utmost, and I ask you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, we were talking about the process of investigations, for example, in your jurisdiction, and we had come to your explanation of why you would try to avoid re-interviewing witnesses more than once but that sometimes it might -- it might be necessary to do so. Now, in the context of these investigations, there might also be some search and seizure operations in which you might recover some documentary evidence. Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a specific type of investigation that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You know, your evidence has covered general criminal investigative procedures. I'm trying to, as briefly as possible, review my understanding, generally speaking, of what might be done and do a comparison to the process that was undertaken here.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's probably no comparison because the rules in my jurisdiction for search and seizure involve the filing of affidavits and obtaining search warrants from the court before seizure of evidence other than seizure incidental to arrest or some of the specific caveats to the search and seizure laws in the United States may apply, so it's -- it is a different system of justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, assuming the suspect is a fugitive, there will be, I suppose, a search operation conducted for the fugitive which might be running simultaneous to the actual substantive investigation. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what would you do to protect your witnesses while you are searching for the fugitive?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a different system again. If we have some reason to believe that the witnesses are in danger, they may be put under police protection, but that's very rare.
