Other than that, I mean, there's no protection per se granted to witnesses or victims of crimes in my jurisdiction, but we don't have the same issues to deal with that you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if a crime scene is not secure, or, let's say, if part of it is not secure, you will continue other aspects of the investigation, I presume, those that you can do until such time as you can secure the site. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And I suppose in your jurisdiction and in your experience, there has never been a case where due to security risks you are physically unable to investigate the crime scene until years after the crime took place.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have cold case scenes like this but for other reasons, being, you know, a body or bodies may be dumped in the desert in our part of the world and not discovered for some time, you know, several years down the road. But once they are discovered, then we would work the crime scene as we've described in testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So what would you do in a situation where you had to investigate a case involving a fugitive through interviewing witnesses, and you did not have a photo of the fugitive?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would try to obtain the best possible description of the individual, and there's going to be -- somewhere in this community, there's going to be someone that knows him to the extent that I can rely on their description. It's going to be perhaps an associate, perhaps a relative. Perhaps there's a photograph. There could be a police record somewhere of when -- in this particular case when he was active with the police, when he was mobilised. There should be some sort of documentation somewhere, if we look, that will have his physical description.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what do you do -- would you do any kind of identification procedure with a witness who knew the accused very well, back home?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So if they're on a -- what we would call a first-name basis in our country, if they are closely associated with one another and they have more than a casual acquaintance, I would probably rely on that identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that there is a difference between conducting an internal investigation and conducting other types of criminal investigations; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mechanics are the same. The purpose is different, but the mechanics of how investigations are conducted are basically the same, whether it's an internal investigation or it's a criminal investigation. It doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you have quite a bit of experience managing internal investigations. I presume that the internal investigations that you managed, that the officers conducting that investigation would have been privy to a great deal of internal information. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If by internal information you're referring to document statements, standard operating procedures, confidential statements that were taken as part of the investigation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So by analogy, then, in this case, actually the task you were asked to do by the Defence team for Milan Lukic was in fact an internal investigation into the OTP methodology of its investigation. Would you say that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say there are a lot of similarities between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you told us before that one of the first things you would do back home in an investigation is to secure the ground, this is something that's normally done by the APD; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So following a crime, there is the ability for you to - you as the APD, let's say - to coordinate with as large a police team as necessary to ensure the security of the site, including security of APD personnel, security of victims and witnesses, et cetera. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little misleading when you say as large a team as necessary because we all have our restrictions as far as personnel available to help us. But generally speaking, we have enough officers on duty to generally secure a crime scene and ensure that there's no contamination of the scene while the investigators arrive and they are briefed on the situation, and the forensics teams are briefed on what information the investigators have, and then they just -- they go their separate ways and do their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So have you ever faced a time where you had to call in the military or the National Guard or some other security organ to secure a crime site --

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- for the APD to investigate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And this is -- this is perhaps in a way something that you might take for granted in your jurisdiction, that for the most part, barring some very huge calamities such as, I don't know, the World Trade Centre disaster or something, that the APD will be able to secure its own criminal investigation sites. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: APD would be able to do that. However, that consideration was taken into account by me when I was reviewing the documents and the overall case. I fully understand that this was a war zone, and I'm sympathetic to that fact. I also understand that standard operating procedures are a guideline rather than a rule or rule of law. The problem is if you're going to vary the procedure, there needs to be some documentation as to why you didn't perform the tasks that you performed. So if I can just take that one step further for you, let's hypothetically say that there's an officer-involved shooting. There's a gun battle similar to the -- if you're familiar with the armed robbery of the banks in California. It's been on television for several years. That basically was a running street battle between the Los Angeles Police Department and the bank robbers. It's almost impossible given that scenario to totally secure that crime scene because there are too many civilians; there's too much going on at that scene. But at some point in time, at some point in time, we -- the Los Angeles Police Department was able to secure that scene to the point where that scene could be processed properly. So my contention is at some point in time, the scenes at Visegrad were secure enough that the crime scene teams could have gone in and processed that evidence safely, certainly more safely than could have done in 1994, but at some point in time prior to 2009 they could have gone in and processed that scene and possibly obtained some evidence that would be of interest to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in studying this case, certainly you became quite familiar with the context of the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would that be correct? And so you will know that the country suffered a three-and-a-half-year civil war with large-scale ethnic cleansing. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you will know that between approximately March and July of 1992, the Bosnian Muslim population of Visegrad dropped from 63 per cent down to less than 5. Would you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm asking him if he knows it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... knows it. It's either within his knowledge or not. Is that within your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those specific numbers are not within my knowledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the whole of Bosnia as of 2005, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross, there were still more than 14.000 persons listed as missing?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard numbers similar to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony you talk about Dr. Clark's work, and on the last page of your report you state: "If the investigators had used the same techniques described by Dr. Clark and had documented their procedures and findings, the Prosecution's case would be much, much stronger." Do you still stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that, to your knowledge, Dr. Clark was conducting his work as of 1996.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: But in fact, he did not begin conducting his work until 1999, and that's been in evidence in this case. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quotation that I used from Dr. Clark's report is the knowledge that I have, and he says 1999 was the third year of the ICTY exhumation programme, so counting backwards three seasons -- now, the question is what is a season. Are we talking spring, summer, fall, when the ground is not frozen, or are we talking back three years? I assume he's going back three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that -- you used the word "perfect" in describing Dr. Clark's work in terms of its assistance to the investigation. Now, did you receive any information, have you been provided with any information about forensic examinations in Visegrad being contemplated, but security did not permit that? Did you receive any of that information?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you actually did not receive any information about the reasons why or why not certain steps were taken in the forensic analysis of the site; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if you had been presented, hypothetically speaking, with some testimony from the head of the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons which said that there was strong evidence that bodies from Pionirska and Bikavac had actually been physically removed and buried somewhere else, would that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object. Improper hypothetical. Amor Masovic was suppressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think as a hypothetical question, regardless of how the evidence comes in, I can put a hypothetical --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Assuming facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the question may be put.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So hypothetically speaking, if there had been that kind of evidence, would that factor into your assessment of what might be possible or might not be possible at the site?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have we hypothetically positively identified beyond reasonable doubt that the bodies that were recovered came from that scene? In other words, other than just someone saying that person came from the scene, have we absolutely positively identified that person as one of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, when I ask you the question, I'm asking you about factors you take into consideration in drawing your conclusions. So would it be a factor that you would want to consider if there had been evidence that the bodies from those sites have been moved? That's the simple question I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a simple question. I'll try to give you a simple answer, in that if that body has been identified as such within a -- within reasonable doubt, then I would certainly consider that information, absolutely. But if there are bodies buried literally all over Visegrad, and I would want some sort of information or more than just a casual, Well, there's a body, I believe it came from Pionirska; I would want some sort of identification to satisfy myself that I was looking at a piece of evidence from that scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, you are aware, I presume, by now, that although the crimes charged in this indictment are alleged to have taken place in 1992, that the Tribunal was established in 1993, and the Office of the Prosecutor in 1994. Were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you were also similarly informed that the war raged in the former Yugoslavia until December of 1995.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you are aware that there was a peace accord signed at that time which divided the country along ethnic lines into the Federation and the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you are aware that unlike the APD, the ICTY did not and does not have its own security force, and it's dependent upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does -- sorry. I'm sorry. Does anyone have a copy of the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So I was saying that the ICTY was dependent upon local law enforcement agencies and NATO to provide security for its field investigations. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you can understand that this means the Tribunal investigators never actually controlled the ground in the way that you might be able to do at home.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And did you know that although the ICTY standard operating procedures placed a paramount priority on protection of witnesses and victims and personnel, that NATO forces did not provide protection for victims or witnesses. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen the SOP from the investigators, so I have no idea what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And are you aware that the first investigative missions carried out by ICTY investigators, not just for the Lukic case but ICTY investigators, took place by helicopter with the investigators wearing body armor and helmets with large-scale armed escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid. What's the basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, these are improper facts, even from a hypothetical perspective, to put before the witness, considering that no evidence of these facts has come in through any witness such as the helicopters and whatnot. And so based on that fact it asks the witness to assume facts not in evidence, and/or it's making the Prosecutor a witness, and she's merely testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness -- I'm sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This witness was asked to -- he even said, to essentially conduct what amounts to an internal investigation of the OTP. He -- of the OTP's investigation. His report says that if he was presented with additional information as to what occurred and what the methodology was and what the factors were, that he might revise his conclusions. As such, I think all of this is directly relevant to Mr. Jenkins's assessment and he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but is it relevant to the case? Now, I have no concern at all about this witness conducting an OTP internal investigation. That's really not that relevant to our exercise here. I don't see the significance of this. Please move on, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And please concentrate on those aspects of his evidence that go to the Prosecution's case, the evidence that it has led, tending to make it more unreliable or less credible. I'm not interested in OTP internal investigation, and in fact, I would characterise it as not proper for the OTP to be using this exercise to defend itself against a so-called internal investigation. That's not our purpose at all here, and I've said enough about this gentleman's evidence for everybody to understand the way that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The OTP does not have to defend its honour as far as I'm concerned. It's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And that is precisely the problem with the report and with that aspect of this witness's extensive evidence about the methodology because if his -- the record is replete with his assessment of the methodology that was undertaken and critiques exactly that methodology without having access to that information. And so that's -- I feel, Your Honours, with the greatest of respect, that since this evidence has been led, unless his evidence, which is impugning the methodology undertaken by the investigators, is going to be stricken from the record that the Prosecutor's office has an obligation, in fact, to contradict Mr. Jenkins's assessment of the methodology simply because this is evidence that was extensively led and contained in his report, Your Honours. The witness has himself said that this was sort of an internal investigation. He comments on things that were missing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the relevance of an internal investigation to the question of the guilt or innocence of the accused, Milan Lukic? I mean, this is something which Mr. Alarid had undertaken. I really question the relevance of it, and I don't know why you need to be bothered with it, unless, as I have said ad infinitum, ad nauseam, that there are aspects of his evidence that affect the credibility, the reliability of the evidence that the Prosecution has adduced. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. One brief moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, you are aware that the accused in this case were at large until 2005; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that they were at large, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you were informed that until that time, it was thought that the accused may still be present in the region?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that. I'm just aware that there was an international warrant issued for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you aware -- I mean, you are aware, I would think, because of the use of pseudonyms, that many witnesses in this case have been very fearful of coming forward to give their evidence. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that you saw the video of the first ICTY mission, which was admitted as an exhibit, 1D84, and you described the military presence that you saw in that video. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you do have some idea what the circumstances were like, and you questioned why the investigators didn't enter, that they stopped at the last moment at the door and didn't go in. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, were you informed that apart from the hostility of the local community to the ICTY, the area was thought to be mined or booby-trapped, and thus NATO did not clear for access into the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't be objecting had they presented a single witness that laid this out, a single investigator to tie the investigation together and explain the difficulties, the trials, the tribulations that the OTP and its staff experienced in putting this case together. But without such foundation, the questions are without merit and not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can resolve this by rephrasing it hypothetically if that will please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, the same question in a hypothetical scenario. Hypothetically speaking, had there been such an assessment that the area was not secure and NATO making that decision, would you alter your comment about this being something that was lacking at that particular investigative mission?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO has the ability to call in bomb technicians or people that can identify the location of the mines. If they felt that it was that insecure, then they should have done a minesweep before they allowed any of the NATO civilian or OTP personnel in that area to begin with. Secondly, there are two windows on the side of that room where video could have been taken through the open windows and at least had some idea of what was inside. Third, if they're that concerned about booby-traps and mines, why were they walking on the first floor in an area that was also unsecured? It could have just as easily been booby-trapped as the door going into the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you've testified --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry. You've testified that there is no comparison, I quote from you, no comparison between investigations back home and this kind of an investigation. And so would you say, then, that if there is an area that can never -- a crime scene area or multiple crime scene areas that can simply never be accessed, let's say they can never be accessed because the security situation never changes, an example, for example, like Darfur may come up. Are you saying that a trial cannot go forward at all based on evidence collected from witnesses outside of that crime scene?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that at all. I mean, there is a possibility that you could put together a circumstantial case. The problem is, as we testified to earlier, is the consistency of the story among the witnesses. There are so many inconsistencies and problems and loose ends with their statements, and in this particular case, not being a hypothetical, those issues could have been addressed as well as the issues of the forensic evidence. So in your hypothetical question, I think the answer is yes. You can proceed with those provided you can get the necessary information to go forward with trial. In the real-world situation here, the investigators had the opportunity to search those crime scenes as they should have and to tighten up the statements and the investigation in such a manner that had been more effectively presented by the Prosecution. I know that sounds bad, but believe me, as a Prosecution-oriented person, I would want to give you the best possible case I could to ensure conviction if in my mind I felt the defendant was the perpetrator, and therein lies the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you would well imagine, or maybe you know for a fact, that the Office of the Prosecutor's investigations unit is full of very highly experienced police officers just like yourself. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know outside of a couple of the investigators that I've seen reports and -- but I don't -- I'm unfamiliar with the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I were to inform you that the current investigations unit in the draw-down phase of the Tribunal has approximately 30 experienced senior-level police officers from 25 different countries, would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would surprise me is they didn't do a better job of investigating this case with that kind of experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So I presume in making that assessment that you asked the Defence team to request a copy of the standard operating procedures?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what was their response?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that no procedures manual was available.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, did the Defence team make that request to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And did you request of the Defence team to interview the chief of investigations, for example, in making your assessment of the methodology?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would object as improper and I would never think I had the right to make such a request. Had I known, I would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to take a position on this, regrettably. I don't think any of this is helpful to the Tribunal in determining the guilt or innocence of Milan Lukic. We may have been led down a path by the Defence introducing this evidence, but why you're responding to it is beyond me. It seems that what you're doing is defending the good name of the Office of the Prosecutor, and I don't believe I should allow the Tribunal's time to be used for that purpose. If you have questions to ask him, again, for the hundredth or thousandth time, where his evidence, the evidence that he gave in-chief might have affected your case, where his evidence bored a hole in your case, put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the final line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it is irresponsible of me to sit here and allow the Tribunal's time to be spent with your asking questions that only affect the good name and reputation of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Then what I would submit, then, is that the report is, at least in those portions, not admissible because the final conclusion is that a failure on the part of the investigators to live up to their professional responsibilities not only fails those left behind, but it fails the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's a question of the weight that we attach to it. It's a question of the weight that we attach to it. It's premature for me to tell you what weight I would attach to that statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- but I don't think it affects the admissibility of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll move on to different topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, are you aware that memorialising interviews with witnesses is done in a wide variety of ways in a wide variety of jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And even within the US, in some jurisdictions witness statements are never recorded.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's speculation on my part, but I assume that's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in your report on page 4, you describe factors that you considered or that could be considered in assessing witness credibility in your opinion, and you mention that one factor might be whether a witness might have a particular motive for providing a particular testimony. You suggest that a witness who is a relative of a victim might have a particular motive for providing false testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's a variety of reasons why individuals come forward if they have no direct knowledge of the incident, and I have since learned since the time this report was given that the Court allows hearsay, and that really speaks to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So when you said that one factor is whether a relative of a victim might have a particular motive for providing false testimony, you were not talking about a relative who was an eye-witness or, let's say, another surviving victim, but, rather, somebody who has no direct knowledge of the actual incident?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So mightn't it have been appropriate to include that caveat in your report when you described this as a factor to be taken into account?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's inclusive in the overall critique. Each witness has to be assessed as to what they have to say, how they came upon the information, and how that information then has been brought forward. There's always the possibility of witness contamination, particularly in this group because we've had so many people displaced and taken to refugee camps, families have reconnected, stories have been told and repeated to the point where, even if by accident, if by accident there is a misidentification and someone says, This person committed such and such a crime, that is taken as the truth, and all of a sudden everyone seems to repeat that whether it's true or not. And it could be simply accidental misidentification and not intentional. So you really have to get to the root of how the witnesses obtain that information and who they've told. It's kind of like a coffee-klatsch thing where, you know, everyone gets together and they talk about the events of the day, and everyone just kind of assumes the other person is telling the absolute truth even though they may have -- because of their observations or their biases or whatever, may see the events slightly differently than someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, going along these lines of motives for giving false testimony, someone who is related to an accused would be likely to also be biased toward them and possibly offer false testimony. Would you say that would be correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you testified about victims groups and how membership in victims groups might be a factor to take into account. You testified that a victim who might be eligible for reparations following an armed conflict might be motivated to fabricate evidence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So this suggests that in your opinion, a reparations regime or a victim reparations regime would incentivise victims to perjure themselves.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the possibility is there. I'm not saying that this is absolutely the case because I have no evidence one way or the other. I'm simply saying that that is a consideration that should be taken into account when you're reviewing the witness's statement. The country is very poor. People have lost their property. They've lost all of their belongings, and the reparation is a very important part of getting them back on their feet and reestablishing their lives. But it's also a tremendous motive, when you think about it, if I have nothing and if I can come forward and join this group and give testimony and in turn receive reparation in exchange for my testimony, then this needs to be weighed. It needs to be considered. The information that the witness gives may be true and correct, but then again, it just needs to be weighed out and see if the information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So hypothetically speaking, if there were an International Tribunal which set up a victims trust fund at the same time as prosecuting the cases, you would suggest that that might call into question the entirety of evidence in that kind of a context?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Again, I think you just have to be aware of that circumstance and the particular station in life that this person has. Do they still have their property? It's just a motive that needs to be considered, and if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there one at the ICC, such a fund?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, there is, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is. But if I were a lawyer for the Defence at the ICC and you produced a witness who had received money from this fund, I would still cross-examine him about it. It goes to credibility. So the witness is perfectly correct, but nothing has been said here that is new. I don't know why we need to be told about it. It does go to credibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, if a statement was given to an investigator prior to the time that that victim either received funding or even became eligible to receive funding through a victim group, would this change your assessment of whether or not that factor should be considered?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you want to consider all of the factors that are possible, and this list is not certainly a disqualifier, if you will, but these are merely guidelines that the investigator should keep in the back of their mind as they're talking with the witness, and to help filter or to help identify the information. Why is the information being given? Is the information true, correct, all of the -- just to check the veracity of the witnesses and make sure that the best possible information comes forward to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, Mr. Jenkins, you would probably agree that providing to witnesses prepared statements for them to sign - hypothetically speaking - would not only be contrary to a professional code of ethics for an investigator or an attorney but could also potentially be prohibited by law. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So hypothetically speaking, if you were to discover that a particular case had been primarily investigated by somebody who did just that, that fact could call into question the integrity of that investigation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, I read through the lines in your report that if you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It depends how the signed statement is presented, in my view. If you have a signed statement and you take it to a person and you take the person through it bit by bit and the person agrees or disagrees with it, what's wrong with that? Eventually it will be his statement. Or are you positing that the potential witness is just presented with a signed statement and he signs it without any questions being asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And perhaps I should have been more clear that this would be prior to the investigator having met that witness before, so prior to the investigator having knowledge of what that witness's evidence would be, upon the first meeting. That was the context in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And I presume, Mr. Jenkins, that's the context in which you answered?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my jurisdiction, that would be totally improper. In the context of the Court's jurisdiction, I understand the rules are different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if you saw two or more witness statements which appeared to be very similar in wording, content, sequence, order, et cetera, I think you even addressed this, mightn't you conclude that these witnesses had maybe gotten together and coordinated their evidence?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's something to consider.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, what would you say about a scenario, hypothetical scenario, where an attorney for one of the parties was also serving as an interpreter for interviews with witnesses?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean putting the attorney in a situation where they are a witness themselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is that what --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, beyond the scope of direct examination, relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It goes directly to the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, then I renew my motion to name the Office of the Prosecutor for every Prosecutor that sat in with an interpreter on a single witness's statement, and especially where statements changed over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alarid. I'll allow the witness to answer the question, but for my part, I don't see that it takes the matter much further, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think we can accept Mr. Jenkins's reply that he already gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jenkins, you testified yesterday that in your report you wrote that the bridge was unlit.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: But now you testified that the bridge was in fact lit.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I amended the report as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And why did you originally say that the bridge was unlit?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the -- at the hotel that we were staying at when we were in Visegrad is immediately next to the bridge. We are within 50, maybe a hundred metres of the bridge, and in the two nights that I spent there walking around in the area, I had never -- looking at the bridge, it never registered with me that the bridge was lighted. It was dark. It wasn't until I subsequently saw the photograph that we presented yesterday which I actually saw that there were lights on the bridge, and that was -- I saw that photograph two weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I say that's an example of a relevant issue. Finally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you made that assessment of the bridge being unlit in the context of assessing the evidence of VG-114.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you said: "She alleges the incidents occurred every night, but the bridge is unlighted." Unlit.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you took an observation that you made in 2009, and you used that to comment on the credibility of a witness's testimony from 1992, a witness's evidence relating to events in 1992.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a little bit more to it than that, counsellor. When we were in Visegrad, we had occasion to go to an area which is immediately above the old bridge that provides an unobstructed view back to the new bridge where these alleged crimes took place, and I took a photograph of that. When I got back to my office in Albuquerque, using Google Earth I pulled up the area around Visegrad, and from the photograph that has been presented in evidence that marks the spots, it's kind of a black-and-white photograph that marks Bikavac, Pionirska, the old police station, you can get a sense of the layout of the land. So using Google Earth, I took one of the tools that's in that programme and measured in metres from the Bikavac fire scene the approximate area where the witness lived to the centre of the new bridge, and that is a distance of 1.4 kilometres. And to the best of my knowledge, not having gone to the actual location where VG-115 was at during this incident, so I can't say whether or not it was a totally unobstructed view, but I can say that from the scene at Bikavac, you cannot see the new bridge. So I hope that's some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So, sir, this is actually a perfect example. You wrote a report as an expert, and in court you made two changes to that report on the record. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, the Defence asked you about those changes, and the Prosecution has an opportunity to ask you about those changes; correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And now the Chamber can ask you questions if they wish, and ultimately, they will make the final determination of what weight to give that particular assertion; correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your evidence has been tested in a court of law, and based on this testing, an assessment will be done by the Chamber of your evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if someone were to be given your report alone without the corrections that you made in court, and let's say those corrections went to a very serious matter at issue in the case, they would not be getting the full story. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And objection, Your Honour. Relevance, beyond the scope, and he's asking for speculation, everything in the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you permit two more question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear the actual question. She hasn't actually reached the meat of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, if you notice in the second paragraph I leave open the option, as you had pointed out earlier, to re-examine any evidence that came to my attention from the time that we were in Visegrad up to and including the time of testimony. Now, the corrections that were made in the report were corrections that I found myself and wanted to make sure that I gave the Prosecution all of the information that is available. Now, as to the question of the -- I guess you would want -- probably from the Prosecution's side, you would want to categorise this as somewhat misleading. I, on the other hand, would characterize it as at the time the report was written, I had a good-faith report submission, and I felt the information in the report at that time from cover to cover, side to side, was true and correct. Since that time I found on my own volition two errors that I felt needed to be addressed to the Court so that they could weigh the evidence appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Precisely. So now taking from what exactly you just said, you testified that what you were provided with in making your assessment of the Prosecution's case was, and I quote from yesterday: "That included witness statements, and primarily that's it. I mean, there were no other reports or documents to review or to support." Now, you also said that you reviewed some photographs, and of course you described your visit to the crime scene. That was the evidence that you looked at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you had a very -- you described the amount of material as quite voluminous.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And it would have been quite a challenge, I presume, to read every single word of all the material you were given; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, of the statements that you were given, were you informed which statements were taken by the Office of the Prosecutor, which ones were taken by other law enforcement agencies, and which statements were taken by non-governmental organisations?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not advised of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you informed which of the statements that you reviewed were confirmed under oath before this Chamber and therefore tested in court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. We've given the Prosecution a complete list of the statements that we gave, and I think the witness can read. And I believe on the top of every one of those statements, that information is on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is the Defence counsel giving testimony -- an alternative answer to what Mr. Jenkins --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I seem to be put in that position constantly and this line of questioning considering the fact it is, does put me in the position of being a witness, considering the allegations and the basis thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Over and over again, the Defence has been the basis of slander by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, please sit. Witness, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment. My question was, were you informed which of the statements you were given had been confirmed under oath and tested in court and which ones had not?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And so you were also not told which of those statements you reviewed had been admitted and accepted by the Chamber and which ones had not?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I looked at all the statement in their totality. If I had multiple statements for one witness, I examined all of the statements side by side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In fact, having reviewed carefully the material that was given to you by the Defence, it seems to me that with the exception of one, and now maybe two, witness testimony from this trial, you did not review, generally speaking, the witness testimony in this case.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So your opinion as to inconsistencies in witness evidence is based purely upon review of preliminary and sometimes unconfirmed statements of witnesses taken by the Office of the Prosecutor and by other agencies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements I reviewed were statements that were taken along the way, depending on when the witness was first identified as having information, so I guess the short answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So your opinion as to the "failure to test the witness information," which is on page 8, and your "rush to judgement" by the investigators is something you arrived at without having the benefit of having reviewed the trial record; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I did not -- I did not have the trial record available to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So any corrections that any of those witnesses may have made before this Chamber in good faith to their prior statements was not something that you were provided with in your assessment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection to the characterization of good faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It was because Mr. Jenkins commented on his good-faith corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point is a very valid one. Let us hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My evaluation of the evidence or of the statements that we're discussing here without the trial record simply was to test the side-by-side credibility of the witnesses, how many different stories did the witnesses tell, did the evidence that was evident in photographs and through our site visits, did it match what the witnesses were saying, but as to any corrections that were made in Court, I was not privileged to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Your Honour, for the record, I felt specifically with this particular witness, given the range of his expertise, I thought it would be improper to give him the current trial testimony because to bring him in here and have him comment on said testimony would be asking him to interfere with your purview in the court, and I figured it would receive a proper objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus. How much longer, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would say maximum 15 minutes, maybe less. I'll really try my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then will there be any re-examination, Ms. O'Leary?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we maybe have five to ten questions. It could be completed in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Jenkins, some of these issues of testing witness credibility, motives, and all the factors that you describe need to be taken into account may very well have all been tested out here at trial by the parties, such that the totality of that witness's evidence including all of the factors you've included are before the Chamber. Isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And would you agree that if you had been, as you provide in your report, if you had been provided with the trial record where you could see which statements were admitted and which weren't, which ones were confirmed, where the alterations were made, how the witness's testimony -- evidence was tested at court, you might have drawn completely different conclusions; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: One brief moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, we alluded earlier today to the criticism that the APD has come under over the years, and you said that this is common to most police departments. Would you say that's correct?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In fact, the APD has come under quite substantial criticism for cases relating to destruction or disappearance of evidence and also quite a large number of alleged criminal cases committed by APD police officers over the years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the relevance, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It will be two questions, Your Honours, and it goes to Mr. Jenkins' understanding of realities faced in investigations. He has assessed the investigation here, so it will be two questions covering this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The realities of investigation here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No. He is commenting on the integrity of the investigation. It is two questions going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an idea approximately how many cases, how many criminal cases were brought against APD police officers during your time within the APD?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my entire tenure?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can think of six or seven cases from the time I began until I left the department where criminal charges were brought.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you estimate approximately how many lawsuits were brought against the city or the APD relating to conduct of police officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you coming to the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm going to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness to answer that one question? Then I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because many of the complaints that are filed or the notices that are filed are handled by the city's legal department before they ever get to -- before they ever got to my office, and before my time as -- my appointment to the rank of deputy chief, I was not in that chain of command, so I really have no idea how many lawsuits were filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have just two more questions for you. If you had been provided with the full trial record and if it had been possible, also, to review the standard operating procedures, to have perhaps an interview with the chief of investigations, to review standards that are used in international criminal investigations, is it possible that the conclusions you reach in your report might have been entirely different than the ones that you actually did reach?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we're speaking hypothetically?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hypothetically, anything's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you would agree, then, as Judge Robinson discussed earlier that even in a case where there has been perhaps an imperfect investigation, there could still be enough evidence to prove guilt?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm advised that it's -- we should return at 2.15 because I, in the break, will be given a lot of information to assist me in the management of the case and the decisions for next week, so we'll adjourn. That doesn't mean, Ms. O'Leary, that you should take longer than is necessary in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just request -- and it may be relevant for redirect on this witness, I request a clarification from the Prosecution as to whether or not they objected to the introduction of the SOPs that we had available through Mr. Ib Jul Hansen, or did they consent and stipulate to their admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's SOP?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Standard operating procedure, and they -- because during the last question in litany -- this witness had the opportunity to review the SOPs of the Office of the Prosecutor investigators as posed to them, and I believe the Prosecution objected to the introduction of that, but I could be mistaken. That's why I'd ask for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Alarid can check the transcript as easy as any of us. I wouldn't want to rely on my memory. We've had many witnesses now in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. You heard that, Mr. Alarid. We are adjourned until 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could have 1D216 on the screen right away and that related to the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: I can ask you a couple of other questions in the meantime while it comes up, Mr. Jenkins. You were asked about if you'd seen any of the trial testimony in this trial. When an investigator is looking at a file, does he typically have the benefit of trial testimony?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: In discussing the record of the interviewing processes, and there were some questions about when you would record, I believe you mentioned the gravity is weighed and involved in whether it would be recorded, when can you give an example or when can you imagine that you in your own jurisdiction would not record a witness statement?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a low-level property crime perhaps you might not record it but certainly in a homicide investigation, the witnesses, suspect, those would all be recorded and saved for posterity. Even though the statement that's actually taken may be drafted by the investigator, reviewed by the witness, and signed, but there is a -- there is a recording of the interview and a recording of the session where the statement is taken, that is preserved and tagged into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. There is now the photograph on the screen that you indicated was the Varda scene and you had marked on. Can you give us an idea of what you saw when you were there as being the square footage of the entire factory, rough estimate of how big it is?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's millions of square feet. It's huge. I'm not sure how far back beyond the factory the property goes. If we are talking about the square footage or square metres of that entire facility, I have no idea. It's immense.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. But in relation to the size of that property, if the charges are, as in the indictment here, that two people entered the factory and forced seven men to go to the river-bank, how many people would you expect to undertake such an activity of going into a property of this size and undertaking --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I believe this is beyond the scope of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doesn't arise, Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Regarding other hypotheticals that you heard today, there was a hypothetical posed by the Prosecution that the bodies could have been moved, and they had wondered if you had taken that into consideration. Can you also imagine a possibility, then, that these two fires did not happen at all?

utterances.speaker: CLIFFORD JENKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a distinct possibility as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for coming today, Mr. Jenkins.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions but I do want to move to admit his full report, the full photo and index that was an addendum and filed, and renew the request to admit the two statements of VG-31 as relevant to the testimony heard here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit his report, the photo and index that was an addendum and filed. What are the two statements of VG-31?

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: VG --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. O'Leary can correct me if I'm wrong, one, I believe, was an ICTY statement; one was the statement taken by the Bosnian authorities. I think we've discussed this matter before and so though there is a general exception to hearsay where lex specialis dictates that where there is a specific provision in the rules to deal with this, and this is written evidence, those are the procedures that would be followed. Otherwise, both parties could call a single witness and introduce reams of recorded statements, the Chamber would be denied opportunity to evaluate their credibility and the parties would be denied the opportunity to cross-examine those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this case, I would just add that this is very specific to the underlying testimony that was heard here today, both in direct and in cross, as far as the materials he reviewed and how it affected his investigative eye on the situation of Varda.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to that, I would say that Mr. Jenkins has commented on the specific portions of the statement that he found relevant. They are a matter of the record. I think he may even have para-phrased some sections, so I don't believe there's any need to introduce the other portions of the statement. Again, this was a person that was on the witness list of the Defence. They expressed some difficulties in contacting the person, but it seems that they made the decision not to call them when the Chamber put a limit on the number of total witnesses that could be called. So it was a strategic -- not sure of the reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which of the 92s you say the statement could have been admitted under?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would submit that either 92 bis or 92 ter an application could be made. If they could not contact the witness, I think then that the appropriate way to proceed would be 92 quater, give us an opportunity to evaluate how genuine the efforts were to contact this witness. I don't know whether they ever made a request of the Bosnian government or whatever country -- the government of whatever country they believed person lives in, for their assistance in contacting the witness, or is it simply that they have took cursory efforts to call a phone listing and were unsuccessful. I think its admission under 92 quater would be very dependent upon the significance of the efforts to locate the witness and secure their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are saying it can't be admitted under 89 -- the provision, is it 89(F), the provision for written statements, because there is a lex specialis, and that is what the 92 provisions were intended to deal with, specifically. No, we have a lot of case law on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, 89(F) -- I think the plain reading of 89(F): "The Chamber may receive the evidence of a witness orally or, where the interests of justice allow, in written form." I mean, I guess I would read that, Your Honour, as a witness in the case, not any witness of any statement. I think to give that the meaning -- I'm not familiar with the jurisprudence arising out of this particular section, but it would seem to me any interpretation of this that in effect gave the Chamber broad authority to simply conduct a trial by adopting statements that didn't comport with the requirements of 92 bis or quater, I would have difficulty understanding that that is the rationale underlying the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm still going to reserve on it and I'll give the decision on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record, I mean, I feel -- I find it really difficult to understand why the Prosecution would take a witness that they achieved VG and pseudonym status for, that is tendered despite the fact that it was ICTY witness that achieved VG status for, they tendered this information in a batch of disclosures that comes to us in August, after the trial started, and then continue to obstruct our ability to present this witness when the reality is this witness is a pseudonym witness under their, really, control. They have access to the witness, they have the 20 offices in 25 countries or 30 investigators that can run all over the world and assist us, and yet we've been forced to play hide the ball with some really relevant testimony. And the fact that they should move to exclude it under a technicality at this juncture considering the matter of which it was tendered and the fact that this is their witness, this is their witness and they would hide from that fact by objecting to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- in a court where hearsay is admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... so my silence isn't misinterpreted. Much of what Mr. Alarid says. I would take great issue with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jenkins, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, now the report of the witness which is 1D22-0696 will become Exhibit 1D218. And photo annex, both of which have been marked for identification today as 1D211 and 1D214, will become Exhibit 1D219. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to discuss some matters relating to the programme for next week. Everything, Mr. Alarid, appears to hinge on whether the accused will give testimony or not. So we have prepared two programmes, two schedules. One on the basis that he will testify; the other on the basis he will not testify. And I would like you to tell me now what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've scheduled a four-hour meeting with the witness on Tuesday morning to facilitate a proofing and/or final determination of that fact. So I can't give you a final answer. I think it would be proper for me to even guess at this moment given the testimony that's presented, but that was going to be the -- we were going to use that break as the impetus to explore that at length. Tuesday 1 to 4, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why are you not meeting with him on Monday in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because we had court scheduled, Your Honour, and we didn't want to presume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have witnesses for Monday then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We -- we just received information that these two subpoenaed witnesses that we did achieve service on have been contacted and they -- Milian [phoen] just said that while we were -- you stayed in here. Over the break we just received some word on that, Your Honour, that the two subpoenaed witnesses that have been served have been contacted and they are facilitating their appearance as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm told not for Monday. Visas have been requested, they travel on Wednesday and so they will be able to testify on Thursday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Then we would meet with the client on Monday, absolutely then. We'll set up several hours for him, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So this is the position then, Mr. Alarid. So you have all of Monday to interview the accused. You must let us know by 4.00 p.m., no later, on Monday, whether he will testify, because if he is going to testify, then he will have to start on Wednesday. On Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm looking at the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are still hoping to have Wednesday afternoon as well. But we must know by 4.00 p.m. on Monday whether the accused is going to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Fair enough. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just ask that with your directive also include notice to the Prosecution whether or not he will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you will of course notify --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Notify everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that there's no court then on Monday, nor on Tuesday because of the security measures for the conference next door. And it means, then, that we will meet on Wednesday at 10 to 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So Monday by 4.00 p.m., the Chamber will be informed as well as the Prosecutor by the Defence as to whether the accused Milan Lukic will testify. We will adjourn until Wednesday at 10 minutes to 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If could I just raise just two matters briefly. Your Honour, I see from the schedule that if he does not testify, the Chamber is expecting rebuttal witnesses here next Friday. This would be the third time now that the witnesses have changed -- victim witnesses completely lost their patience with us, and I fear that some of these witnesses that have rescheduled their work. I would ask the Chamber to consider -- I see there are some flextime built into the schedule. Yesterday the Chamber advised us that we would start our rebuttal case on the 6th of April, we made arrangements with the witnesses for that, and that's all been done. I'd ask the Chamber to consider allowing Friday, if he does not testify, to be flextime, I think the parties have plenty of work to occupy us and if we could just fix the Monday as a definitive date for the Prosecution evidence, I believe it still fits well within the Court's goals for concluding the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I'm reminded that we haven't yet received from you any notification of about rejoinder witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. The only I think at this point in time we would reserve -- if we were able to effect subpoena service on the remaining witnesses, we would consider them rejoinder. They've already been allowed on the case in-chief and should we have the time, that's when I would prefer to bring them, but we don't have anyone else arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today is the last day to notify the Chamber of any rejoinder witnesses. The other thing too, is, Mr. Alarid, that the Defence needs to be aware that its case will definitely be concluded next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We are happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By Friday if not before. Not go beyond Friday. Mr. Groome, as to your proposal to make Friday flextime, I'm reminded that the Trial Chamber may have two Chamber witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm advised it would not be advisable to change Friday as the flextime, and I'm sorry about the witnesses being told so many times, but in view of the court schedule, it does not appear to be wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as always we'll do our best to accommodate the Chamber, just please recognise if we don't find out until the end of Monday, Tuesday is a lost day, it will be Wednesday before victim witness can then begin to book the tickets and change the -- and I don't know how long it takes but I imagine they may find -- they may not have complete success starting out Wednesday morning to try to arrange all the travel. But we will of course do our best, Your Honour. Your Honour, just one other matter I'd like to address to the Chamber. Mr. Alarid filed an application for bar table motion on the 25th. The Chamber has asked us to file our response by Wednesday, the 1st of April. In looking at this motion, there's an -- it all seems to be based upon an RFA and the RFA is discussed. It's an RFA dated the 5th of February, 2009, but it doesn't have the response attached to the motion, it would be very helpful to have the response so that we know exactly what it is we are dealing with. Further, there are a number of documents that there is no translation there. There are also two annexes in the application, both listed annex C, with different documents and we are having a difficult time sorting all of this out. There are two -- also two pages ending in 0586 and 0587 which are completely blackened, its impossible to read anything on them. So we are asking the Chamber to direct the Milan Lukic Defence to at least refile a courtesy copy of the document that does have -- is a complete document that we can respond to. It's kind of hindering our ability to draft our response the way it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can clarify. I can't clarify as to the blackened documents, I don't know what order they were added to the annex, but I can clarify as to the RFA. Essentially, Your Honours, we sent a request for assistance to the Visegrad municipality asking for any and all documents that have been sent to the Prosecution response to Prosecution requests for assistance, and the documents that comprise the annex to our motion are precisely those documents that we received back from the Visegrad municipality. There was not a written response that at least that I received. These documents arise from my visit to the Visegrad municipality where -- and I was shocked to find out that the Office of the Prosecution had in their possession documents confirming a part of the Defence case that we had never been disclosed and that -- that was when they advised me that I should send a formal request to obtain these documents. These were responses to requests for assistance by the Office of the Prosecutor which the Prosecution had received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the bottom line, as Mr. Alarid likes to say, is what? Are you able to provide these missing articles from the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll take a look at the filing and see what is missing, what is black, I'll be more than happy to provide a full copy of what I received, but there is no letter, per se, to me from Visegrad. It's these documents that I received from the Visegrad municipality that are the annexes, but I will make sure a complete set is provided to them today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept Mr. Ivetic's explanation and thank him for it. The two translations we are missing are 1D22-0552, and 1D22-0564; and the two illegible documents are 1D22-0586 and 1D22-0587. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, that's on the transcript, Mr. Ivetic. We are adjourned until Wednesday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of April, 2009, at 8.50 a.m.
